Fix #28725: only write db_identifier and checkpoint_iteration in the WAL header for storage v1.4.0+

101) and a v1.4.0 file (still contains field 102). I also verified that

title: Pin the vortex extension's clang-devel install and skip C++20 module scanning
body:
### Problem

Since about 13:00 UTC today (2026-11-13) the job **Build extensions / Build Linux (external, linux_amd64)** fails on every PR run while building the out-of-tree vortex extension:

```
Scanning .../vortex_extension.cpp for CXX dependencies
/bin/sh: /usr/bin/clang-scan-deps-21: No such file or directory
```

### Cause

duckdb-vortex's `CMakeLists.txt` runs `yum install -y clang-devel clang` at CMake configure time inside the Linux CI container. The manylinux_2_28 (AlmaLinux 8) image ships clang 21.1.8, and because vortex sets `CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20`, CMake has already identified the compiler as Clang 21.1.8 and picked `/usr/bin/clang-scan-deps-21` for C++20 module scanning before that `yum install` runs. AlmaLinux published the LLVM 22.1.8 module to appstream today, so the same `yum install` now upgrades clang/llvm/lld to 22 mid-configure (11 upgrades, 7 installs), `clang-scan-deps-21` disappears, and the first C++ source scan dies with exit 127. Until yesterday the install was a no-op for clang itself, which is why this only started now.

### Fix

New patch `.github/patches/extensions/vortex/0002-pin-clang-devel-and-skip-module-scan.patch` with two coordinated edits to duckdb-vortex's `CMakeLists.txt`:

1. `set(CMAKE_CXX_SCAN_FOR_MODULES OFF)` next to the other `CMAKE_CXX_*` settings. Vortex uses no C++ modules, so the dependency scanner (and with it `clang-scan-deps-<ver>`) is never needed.
2. The yum branch installs the `clang-devel` matching the already installed clang instead of the newest one, and falls back to the previous unpinned command when clang is absent or that exact package is unavailable:
   ```
   sh -c "yum install -y clang-devel-$(rpm -q --qf '%{VERSION}-%{RELEASE}' clang) || yum install -y clang-devel clang"
   ```
   The apk branch and the `RESULT_VARIABLE` handling are unchanged.

The patch is numbered `0002` and therefore sorts before the legacy unnumbered `pass-variable-through-cmake-not-make.patch`, so it is written against the pinned tag plus `0001` and leaves the legacy patch's context intact.

### Validation

- `make extension-patch-check`: `ok: 21 extensions apply patches, all accounted for`.
- Fresh clone of duckdb-vortex at `f56da1b2`: all three patches apply cleanly in sorted order (`0001`, `0002`, `pass-variable-...`) with `patch -p1 --forward` as `scripts/apply_extension_patches.py` does, and with `git apply`; both sequences produce an identical `CMakeLists.txt`.
- `cmake -S <patched clone>` parses the whole file (fails only at `build_static_extension`, which DuckDB's build provides).
- In the real CI image `ghcr.io/duckdb/duckdb-ci/manylinux_2_28_amd64_rust:20260923-ade72a46`: `rpm -q clang` is `21.1.8-1.module_el8.10.0+4172+b6b13d75`; appstream now offers `clang-devel` 19, 20, 21 and 22.1.8-2. The pinned command installs `clang-devel-21.1.8-1` plus six same-version dependencies, no upgrades; afterwards `clang --version` is still 21.1.8 and `/usr/bin/clang-scan-deps-21` is present. With a garbled package name yum exits non-zero, so the `||` fallback runs.
- `git diff --check` only flags unified-diff context lines carrying the upstream file's own whitespace, the same as the existing vortex patches.

title: Respect `max_execution_time` in blocking waits
body:
Several places that can run long between interrupt checks noticed the `max_execution_time` deadline late, or not at all:

1. `sleep_ms` and `pg_sleep`: up to ~25 seconds late, so `SET max_execution_time = 1000; SELECT pg_sleep(3);` succeeded.
2. Glob expansion, e.g. `read_parquet('s3://bucket/**/*.parquet')`: completely ignored the deadline.
3. `WaitForAsyncOpen` in the multi-file reader: up to ~2.5 seconds late.
4. The `create_external_resource` poll: up to ~1.3 seconds late.
5. Optimizer passes: noticed the deadline only by chance, with one check per pass.
6. Expanding nested views: noticed the deadline only by chance, with one check per view.

These now call `InterruptCheck()`, which always checks the deadline. The first commit renames the old `InterruptCheck()`, which only reads the clock every 256th call, to `FastInterruptCheck()`, and `BlockingInterruptCheck()` to `InterruptCheck()`.

title: Bound the input of a grouped aggregate whose Top-N orders by the group keys
body:
"The first n groups by the grouping key" is a very common query shape: the first or latest n days of a per-day report, the n smallest ids with their totals, a page of a paginated per-key summary, a preview of a grouped result:

```sql
SELECT user_id, count(*), sum(amount) FROM events GROUP BY user_id ORDER BY user_id LIMIT 10;
SELECT user_id, count(*), sum(amount) FROM events GROUP BY user_id LIMIT 10;
```

Today both aggregate every group of the input and then keep n of them. The Top-N above the aggregate cannot help: its boundary is only known once the aggregate has finished.

This PR adds an optimizer rule, `group_by_top_key`, that bounds the input of the aggregate with a new streaming operator, `TOP_KEY_FILTER`:

```
TOP_N(n, ORDER BY k1 [, k2 ..] [, agg ..])        TOP_N(..)
  PROJECTION*                                       PROJECTION*
    AGGREGATE(k1 .. km; aggs)              ==>        AGGREGATE(k1 .. km; aggs)
      <input>                                           TOP_KEY_FILTER(n, keys: k1 [, k2 ..])
                                                          <input>      (+ a dynamic filter on k1 in the scans)
```

Every thread keeps the n smallest distinct key tuples it has seen; the largest of them is a bound, and the smallest bound of all threads is shared. A row passes if its key tuple is not larger than the bound (ties included). The bound is never smaller than the n-th smallest distinct key tuple of the whole input, so every group that the Top-N can return still receives all of its rows and its aggregates are exact; groups after the bound may be incomplete, but they sort after n complete groups. A prefix of the ORDER BY that consists of group keys is enough, because the order is lexicographic: `ORDER BY k, sum(x) DESC LIMIT n` qualifies with the key `k`. The first key of the bound is also published as a dynamic filter into the scans, with the machinery of the Top-N.

A `LIMIT` without `ORDER BY` over a grouped aggregate may return any n groups. The rule turns it into a Top-N over a group key (the first one that is a plain column, preferring a numeric / VARCHAR one), so that the same filter applies and only the groups that are returned are aggregated:

```
LIMIT(n)                                 PROJECTION*
  PROJECTION*                   ==>        TOP_N(n, ORDER BY k)
    AGGREGATE(k1 .. km; aggs)                AGGREGATE(k1 .. km; aggs)
```

This changes *which* n groups such a query returns (the ones with the smallest keys instead of the first ones of the hash table), which the query leaves open. With an `OFFSET` the query still leaves open which groups are skipped, so it keeps the warning that an `OFFSET` over a result without a guaranteed row order raises (an error with `warnings_as_errors`): the rule raises it when it replaces the `LIMIT`, whose planning raises it otherwise.

### Preconditions

* A Top-N (or a `LIMIT` with a constant limit and offset) with `LIMIT + OFFSET <= 10000` over projections over a grouped aggregate with one grouping set and without `GROUPING()`. A filter (`HAVING`), a window or anything else in between ends the match: such operators have to see every group.
* The ORDER BY keys of the prefix are group keys, reached through the projections by columns, integral casts and the decompression of compressed materialization (which preserve the order). A group key that is an expression (`date_trunc('day', t)`) is computed once in a projection below the filter, and the aggregate reads that column instead of computing the expression twice.
* The filter computes a key for every input row, the Top-N for one row of a group, so an expression *over* group keys (`ORDER BY k + 1`) only qualifies if it has the same value for all rows of a group: it is deterministic, it cannot throw, and it only reads group keys of types whose equal values cannot be told apart. FLOAT and DOUBLE are not such types, also inside nested types: -0.0 and 0.0 are one group, but `1.0 / k` differs for them. Such an expression also has to be cheap (it is evaluated per row instead of per group).
* The key types are an allow-list of the types whose sort keys order like their comparison and are the same for values that group together: integers, DECIMAL, BOOLEAN, DATE, TIME, the timestamps, VARCHAR, BLOB, UUID, ENUM, FLOAT and DOUBLE (-0.0 / 0.0 and all NaNs have one sort key each), and STRUCT / LIST / ARRAY of these. INTERVAL is declined (1 month and 30 days are one group with two sort keys), as is every type that is not listed (TIME WITH TIME ZONE, VARIANT, MAP, UNION, ...). A collated group key is grouped by its collation key and returned through an aggregate, so its ORDER BY does not resolve to a group key and the rule does not apply.
* For the `LIMIT` form the aggregate has aggregate functions (an aggregate without them is a DISTINCT, which the `LIMIT` already stops early), a group key of a supported type is a plain column, and no projection between the `LIMIT` and the aggregate is volatile or can throw: the projections move above the Top-N, where they only see the rows that are returned (a sequence would no longer advance for the rows that an `OFFSET` skips; the limit pushdown declines for the same reason).
* The dynamic filter is only pushed for numeric and VARCHAR keys whose scan column can be compared without a cast that can throw, as for the Top-N, and only if the limit is at most 1/8 of the estimated number of groups.

### Keeping the filter cheap when it cannot help

* A thread only starts to collect keys after it has seen 256 rows per key of the limit; before that its rows pass untouched (a thread that sees few rows never pays for a key set).
* Without a dynamic filter in the scans the operator sees every row, so it can tell whether it helps: a thread that still passes more than 1/8 of its rows after the warm-up stops filtering (passing every row is always correct). This covers limits that return most of the groups.
* While the key set of a thread does not change, offering rows to it backs off exponentially.
* The operator does not cache small chunks. The rows that pass reach the aggregate in the order of the input, so with one thread an aggregate that depends on the order of its input (`list`, `string_agg`, `first`) returns what it returns without the rule; with several threads that order is open with and without the rule. A cache would be unordered here (a pipeline into a hash aggregate is not order-dependent) and would hold a small chunk back while a later full chunk passes. Without it the measured instructions change by at most 0.25% (1 thread, 50 million rows; 0.1% for the example below).

With these, the shapes that cannot profit stay within 1.02x of the instructions without the rule in my measurements (for example `LIMIT 900` of 1,000 groups, `LIMIT 1000` of 1,000 groups, a limit of half the groups with two keys).

### Example

```sql
CREATE TABLE events AS
SELECT (hash(i) % 1000000)::INTEGER AS user_id, (i % 100)::INTEGER AS amount,
       DATE '2024-01-01' + (i % 365)::INTEGER AS day
FROM range(50000000) t(i);

SELECT user_id, count(*), sum(amount) FROM events GROUP BY user_id ORDER BY user_id LIMIT 10;
```

Before:

```
TOP_N                 Top: 10, Order By: user_id ASC
  HASH_GROUP_BY       Groups: #0, Aggregates: count_star(), sum_no_overflow(#1)     ~1,000,000 groups
    SEQ_SCAN          events                                                        50,000,000 rows
```

After:

```
TOP_N                 Top: 10, Order By: user_id ASC
  HASH_GROUP_BY       Groups: #0, Aggregates: count_star(), sum_no_overflow(#1)
    TOP_KEY_FILTER    Keys: user_id ASC NULLS LAST, Limit: 10, Dynamic Filter: true
      SEQ_SCAN        events, Filters: optional: Dynamic Filter (user_id)
```

Timings on this table (release build, in-memory, best of 2 on a shared machine, 8 threads unless noted):

| query | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `GROUP BY user_id ORDER BY user_id LIMIT 10` | 226 ms | 10 ms |
| the same, 1 thread | 1.28 s | 0.07 s |
| `GROUP BY user_id LIMIT 10` | 180 ms | 14 ms |
| `GROUP BY user_id, day ORDER BY user_id, sum(amount) DESC LIMIT 10` | 357 ms | 11 ms |
| `GROUP BY day ORDER BY day DESC LIMIT 10` (365 groups) | 29 ms | 20 ms |

Measured in user-mode instructions at 1 thread over 50 million rows with uniformly distributed keys, `GROUP BY k ORDER BY k LIMIT 10` runs at 0.96x / 0.87x / 0.51x / 0.46x / 0.10x for 100 / 1,000 / 10,000 / 1 million / 10 million distinct keys.

### Known limits

* If the group key reaches the aggregate through a cast that can throw (compressed materialization narrows a `BIGINT` key with a small range, or a short string key), the dynamic filter is not pushed into the scan; the filter operator still removes the rows before the aggregate.
* If the limit covers a large part of the groups and the estimate of the number of groups is far too high, a dynamic filter is pushed that removes little; the operator cannot see that, because it only receives the rows that pass the scan.

### Other changes

* `LogicalTopKeyFilter` / `PhysicalTopKeyFilter` are new operators (serialization, EXPLAIN, physical plan generation, operator visitor).
* The warning about an `OFFSET` over an unordered result moved into a function that the planner of the `LIMIT` and the rule share.
* The dynamic filter push of the Top-N optimizer moved into a function that both rules use. It now returns without a filter if rebuilding the sort key on the scan column needs a cast that can throw; so far this case was an assertion.

### Tests

* `test/optimizer/group_by_top_key.test`: results with the rule disabled and enabled against hand-checked rows (ASC / DESC, NULLS FIRST / LAST, NULL keys, ties, several keys and prefixes, expression keys, DISTINCT, OFFSET, joins and CTEs below the aggregate, 1 and 8 threads), the plans, limits that cover most of the keys, and aggregates that depend on the order of their input (`list`, `string_agg`, `first`, `last`, `any_value`, `arg_min` / `arg_max` with ties) on an input where a group gets one row from each of two chunks and then a full chunk.
* `test/optimizer/group_by_top_key_key_types.test`: keys whose equal values can differ, on tables large enough for the filter to work. Plans: DOUBLE / FLOAT group keys (also in STRUCT and LIST) get the filter, expressions over them do not; INTERVAL and TIME WITH TIME ZONE keys do not; expressions over exact keys do unless they can throw. Results, rule disabled and enabled, 1 and 8 threads: -0.0 / 0.0 in either order of arrival, NaN of both signs, infinities and NULL in every order, nested keys with NULLs inside in every order, INTERVAL, TIME WITH TIME ZONE, collated keys and collated orders.
* `test/optimizer/group_by_top_key_limit.test`: `LIMIT` without `ORDER BY`. The rows of such a query are only pinned through properties that hold for any valid answer, or with the rule enabled where the result is the n smallest keys.
* `test/optimizer/group_by_top_key_limit_offset_warning.test`: `LIMIT` with `OFFSET` and without `ORDER BY` warns with the rule enabled as with the rule disabled (several keys, a key that is not selected, a subquery, `EXPLAIN`); no warning without an `OFFSET`, with `OFFSET 0` or with an `ORDER BY`.
* `test/optimizer/group_by_top_key_guards.test`, `test/optimizer/group_by_top_key_limit_guards.test`: one negative test per precondition next to a positive one (among them volatile and throwing projections above the aggregate of the `LIMIT` form, and a sequence that advances for the row an `OFFSET` skips), results on edge inputs.
* `test/optimizer/group_by_top_key_dictionary.test`: dictionary-encoded and ENUM keys from persistent storage.
* `test/optimizer/group_by_top_key_throwing_cast_filter.test`: no dynamic filter through a cast that can throw.

Skip lists: the plan-pinning files are added to `disable_optimizer.json`, `verify_aggregate_state_export.json` and `variant_order_verification.json` (the configs rewrite the aggregate or the ORDER BY, so the plans differ; results were checked to be unaffected), the ENUM test to the ENUM entry of `variant_order_verification.json`, one file that uses `OFFSET` without `ORDER BY` on purpose to `warnings_as_errors.json`, and the warning test to `force_storage_restart.json` next to the existing test of that warning (the logging settings do not survive the restart between statements).

### Regression check

Rule disabled vs enabled in the same binary (`SET disabled_optimizers`), TPC-H and TPC-DS at SF1 and SF10 and ClickBench: 1 of 22, 26 of 99 and 2 of 43 plans change. Results are identical on TPC-H and TPC-DS SF1 with 1 and 32 threads. On ClickBench one query with a changed plan is a `LIMIT` without `ORDER BY` over a grouped aggregate, which now returns the groups with the smallest keys; the other queries whose output differs between the arms do not contain the rule and are not deterministic: their output also differs between runs of the same arm (ties and row order under a `LIMIT`). Measured in user-mode instructions at 1 thread (`perf stat -e instructions:u`, median of 3), no query with a changed plan is above 1.03x; the geometric mean over the changed TPC-DS plans is 1.00 at SF1 and 1.00 at SF10. The effect on these suites is small, because their grouped Top-N queries aggregate few groups; the example above carries the case.

No expected plan or result of an existing test changes.

title: Let a registered state handle an interrupt instead of failing the query
body:
When a query is run remotely (e.g. motherduck/postgres/quack) that query may complete there, while duckdb at the same time interrupts the query (through Ctrl+C or `max_execution_time`). This can cause an `InterruptError` to be returned to the user, even though a write query actually got fully committed on the server. The local version of this problem has already been addressed by ignoring interrupts during a local commit.  

This extends that approach to remote queries too, by allowing an extension to override `OnInterrupt()` to handle such an interrupt or passed deadline instead, e.g. by forwarding it to where the query runs. Then the local query does not error out, unless the server reports an interrupt error back.

Other behaviour changes that come with it:

1. The sort throws on an interrupt, instead of returning early with partly sorted data and relying on a later check to throw.
2. The sort also stops at the deadline, not only on an interrupt.

title: CREATE EXTENSION REPOSITORY <host>: the host names its repository (#28719)
body:
A repository created without a prefix is named after its publisher's host, and the host says where the repository is:
https://<host>/.well-known/duckdb-extension-repo.json is the same metadata file a prefix serves, and only those fields are read:
```
{"version": 1, "repository_url": "<url>"}
```

From there on it is CREATE EXTENSION REPOSITORY <host> WITH PREFIX '<url>': the signing keys are fetched from the prefix and pinned. The fetch over https from the host is what makes the file the host's own statement; no registry is involved.

Repository names may therefore contain dots (not at the ends, not two in a row), and a host is spelled as dotted words wherever a repository is named:
Examples:
```sql
CREATE EXTENSION REPOSITORY carlopi.github.io;
INSTALL x FROM carlopi.github.io;
LOAD x FROM carlopi.github.io;
DROP EXTENSION REPOSITORY carlopi.github.io;
```
The built-in names stay reserved. A repository remembers the host it was resolved from, shown as the `host` column of
duckdb_extension_repositories().

Repository `carlopi.github.io` is backed by
https://carlopi.github.io/.well-known/duckdb-extension-repo.json, and repoints to the repository at
https://carlopi.github.io/example-duckdb-extension-repository (whose duckdb-extension-repo.json file lives at
https://carlopi.github.io/example-duckdb-extension-repository/.well-known/duckdb-extension-repo.json). That the repository and the extension are baked by the same host its due to convenience of github, but it's a coincidence.

Idea is that the ability to publish a `.well-known` file IS proof of control over an host.

allow_extension_repositories: 'undecided' (the default) lets a repository be created from its host; a repository by prefix still needs 'allowed'. The new 'known_hosts' value sits between 'allowed' and 'forbidden' in the one-way ratchet: only repositories resolved from their host can be added, and only those are trusted for install and load.

Reading a remote metadata file that needs httpfs reports a missing or non-autoloadable httpfs as such, for both forms, instead of a missing file. The debug setting debug_extension_repository_host_base lets tests serve hosts from a directory.

`INSTALL AND LOAD x FROM '<name>'` loads from the repository the install resolved, whether the name was given as an identifier or as a string; before, a string source fell back to a bare load, which never finds an extension installed from a user repository.

Known consequence: a v2.0.0 binary sharing the repository directory lists repositories with an error once a file with a dotted name exists, since it validates every file's name with the old rule; its INSTALL and LOAD, which look repositories up by name, are unaffected. Accepted.

title: Stop rendering expressions as SQL to name relation statistics columns
body:
Closes https://github.com/duckdblabs/duckdb-internal/issues/11281

PR from https://github.com/duckdb-bot/duckdb/pull/107

title: Add an escape_mode option to the CSV reader: 'quote' stops the escape from escaping the delimiter and newlines
body:
This adds an `escape_mode` option to `read_csv` and `COPY ... FROM`. The default, `'all'`, is today's behavior: with `strict_mode = false`, the escape character makes whatever byte follows it literal, including the delimiter and the line break. `'quote'` limits the escape to the quote and escape characters: before anything else the escape is dropped and the byte keeps its meaning, so a delimiter still separates values and a newline still ends the record. This is how Hive/Athena's OpenCSVSerde (and similar line-based readers) treat a `\` escape — files written that way currently read back corrupted: `a\,b` collapses into one field, and a line ending in `\` swallows the following row (`1,\` / `2,b` / `3,c` reads as 2 rows instead of 3).

The change is confined to the state machine: under `'quote'`, the `UNQUOTED_ESCAPE` row transitions to `DELIMITER`/`RECORD_SEPARATOR`/`CARRIAGE_RETURN` instead of staying in the field (multi-byte delimiters and comment characters keep their meaning too); value materialization is untouched since escape removal already drops the escape byte. The option is part of the state machine cache key, flows through the sniffer, and is serialized with a default so existing plans are unaffected. An invalid value gets an error explaining both modes; combining it with an explicit `strict_mode = true` errors (unset `strict_mode` is implied `false`); without an escape character distinct from the quote the option is inert, which keeps the prompt built by `sniff_csv` runnable. Inside quotes nothing changes, and the writer is unaffected.

title: Rewrite aggregates over a single-branch CASE into filtered aggregates
body:
Conditional aggregation is very often written as an aggregate over a `CASE`: pivot-style reports that compute one column per status / weekday / channel (`sum(CASE WHEN status = 'shipped' THEN amount ELSE 0 END)`), counts per category (`count(CASE WHEN .. THEN 1 END)`, `sum(CASE WHEN .. THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`), and it is what SQL generators emit for dialects without `FILTER`. For such an aggregate we currently compute the `CASE` into a vector for every row and update the aggregate state for every row, including the rows that only contribute a NULL or a 0.

This PR adds an optimizer rule, `case_to_filter_aggregate`, that turns these aggregates into filtered aggregates. It builds on #28264: the state is only updated for the rows that match, and aggregates that share a condition evaluate it once per chunk.

### The rewrite

| aggregate | becomes | when |
|---|---|---|
| `f(CASE WHEN c THEN x END)` | `f(x) FILTER (WHERE c)` | `f` is `sum`, `count`, `avg`, `min`, `max`, `bool_and` or `bool_or`: both forms are NULL (0 for `count`) if no row matches |
| `count(CASE WHEN c THEN k END)` | `count(*) FILTER (WHERE c)` | `k` is a non-NULL constant |
| `sum(CASE WHEN c THEN x ELSE 0 END)` | `coalesce(sum(x) FILTER (WHERE c), 0)` | `x` is provably not NULL |
| `sum(CASE WHEN c THEN x ELSE 0 END)` | `CASE WHEN count(*) > count(*) FILTER (WHERE c) THEN coalesce(sum(x) FILTER (WHERE c), 0) ELSE sum(x) FILTER (WHERE c) END` | `x` is nullable: a group in which every row matches and every `x` is NULL is NULL (a sum over NULLs); any other group without a non-NULL matching `x` has a row that contributed the `ELSE 0`. The two counts are shared by all aggregates with the same condition |
| `sum(CASE WHEN c THEN k ELSE 0 END)` | `count(*) FILTER (WHERE c) * k` | `k` is an integer constant |

Where the aggregate returns a row for an empty input (no `GROUP BY`, or a grouping set without columns), the `ELSE 0` forms are wrapped in `CASE WHEN count(*) > 0 THEN .. END`, because the sum over no rows is NULL and not 0.

### Preconditions

The aggregate is left alone if

* it is `DISTINCT`, has a `FILTER` or an `ORDER BY` already, or exports its state;
* the `CASE` has more than one `WHEN`, or an `ELSE` other than NULL (or other than the constant 0 for `sum`);
* the condition is volatile or contains a subquery;
* the `THEN` expression can throw or is volatile: the `CASE` evaluates it for the matching rows only, the filtered aggregate evaluates its argument for every row (so `sum(CASE WHEN is_number THEN s::INTEGER END)` keeps its `CASE`);
* the `THEN` expression is a `FLOAT` / `DOUBLE` constant under `sum` / `avg`: for a constant input vector `sum` adds `value * count` instead of adding the value `count` times, and that is another floating-point number (100 times `0.1` is `9.99999999999998`, `100 * 0.1` is `10.0`). A constant `THEN` is such a vector in every chunk, so the filtered sum would never have the digits of the `CASE` form;
* it is a `min` / `max` over a string or a nested type: these read the vector that the `CASE` produces faster than a slice of the argument (two such aggregates over the same `CASE` measured 1.12x - 1.16x slower as filtered aggregates when 90% or more of the rows match).

The NOT NULL proof for the bare `coalesce` form only follows constants, columns that are proven to be free of NULLs, `+`, `-`, `*` and casts between numeric types. Anything else (a struct field, a list element, a `TRY_CAST`) takes the form with the two counts.

A column is proven with the existing `NotNullExpressionAnalyzer`: a filter or join condition that rejects NULL, or the statistics of the scanned table (which is also how a NOT NULL constraint is seen). The proof has to hold for the rows that the aggregate reads, so the statistics are only consulted where the optimizer itself relies on them:

* not in a plan with a data-modifying CTE (`WITH u AS (UPDATE t SET x = NULL RETURNING x) SELECT sum(CASE WHEN c THEN x ELSE 0 END) FROM t`): the scan reads rows that the statistics did not describe when the plan was made. Statistics propagation is skipped for these plans for the same reason, and they always take the form with the two counts, which is correct for any input;
* not when statistics propagation is disabled.

The table statistics include the uncommitted changes of the running transaction, they still cover NULLs that another connection has overwritten (and checkpointed) while a transaction can read them, and a prepared statement that reads a table is planned again when it is executed. Rows that do not come from a table (a table function, a recursive CTE, the NULL-extended side of an outer join) are never proven NOT NULL.

The rule runs after aggregate reuse and partial aggregate pushdown. These only match aggregates without a filter, so they still see the `CASE`: a pre-aggregation that is pushed below a join stays as it is today.

### Floating-point sums

`sum` / `avg` over a `DOUBLE` argument that is not a constant are rewritten (a `FLOAT` argument is not: its cast to `DOUBLE` sits between the aggregate and the `CASE`). The filtered aggregate adds the same values in the same order as the `CASE` form (the rows of the `ELSE 0` add `0.0`, which changes nothing), so that the digits are the same when the query runs on one thread. With more threads the digits of a `DOUBLE` sum already vary from run to run, in either form.

There is one exception, and it is behaviour of `sum` and not of the rewrite: the constant input vector mentioned above. The `CASE` computes a flat vector and thereby hides a constant vector from the sum; the filtered aggregate receives it, as a hand-written `sum(x) FILTER (WHERE c)` and a plain `sum(x)` do. A column arrives as constant vectors from the one-row side of a cross join and from constant or RLE compressed segments of a persistent table, which is not known when the plan is made. In these cases the result is the one of the hand-written `FILTER` and can differ from the `CASE` form in the low digits: `10.0` instead of `9.99999999999998` for 100 times `0.1` from a one-row table, `9.951039336363154` instead of `9.95103933636457` for the `avg` over half of 1M rows of an RLE compressed column (ungrouped, one thread). For comparison, a plain `sum(x)` over 1M rows of `0.1` is `100000.00000000087`, `100000.00000006249` or `100000.00000133288` today, depending on whether the table is persistent and compressed, persistent and uncompressed, or in memory. Leaving `sum` / `avg` over `DOUBLE` alone instead would give up the rewrite for these columns: the example below with a `DOUBLE` amount runs at 0.71x the instructions of the `CASE` form on one thread, the same as with the integer amount.

The rule has its own optimizer type, so `SET disabled_optimizers = 'case_to_filter_aggregate'` switches it off.

### Two supporting changes

A filter that selects every row should cost as little as no filter, otherwise a condition that happens to be always true makes the rewritten form slower than the `CASE`:

* the statistics propagator drops an aggregate filter that is proven to be true for every row (this also applies to a hand-written `FILTER`), and reports it like the other expressions it removes, so that a column which only the filter read is pruned from the scan;
* the aggregate filter data passes the payload on without slicing it when a chunk passes the filter completely.

With these two, the worst shape I could construct is three numeric aggregates over the *same* `CASE` expression with 99% of the rows matching, at 1.04x the instructions of the `CASE` form; the same shape is at 1.00x with 90% and 0.89x with 50% of the rows matching.

### Example

```sql
CREATE TABLE orders AS
SELECT i % 1000 AS customer, i % 4 AS status, (i * 7) % 100 AS amount
FROM range(50000000) t(i);

SELECT customer,
       sum(CASE WHEN status = 0 THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS open_amount,
       sum(CASE WHEN status = 1 THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS shipped_amount,
       count(CASE WHEN status = 2 THEN 1 END) AS returned,
       avg(CASE WHEN status = 3 THEN amount END) AS avg_cancelled
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer;
```

Before:

```
PROJECTION            CAST(#0 AS BIGINT), #1, #2, #3, #4
  PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY   Groups: #0
                          Aggregates: sum_no_overflow(#1), sum_no_overflow(#2), count(#3), avg(#4)
    PROJECTION            customer,
                          CASE WHEN ((status = 0)) THEN (amount) ELSE 0 END,
                          CASE WHEN ((status = 1)) THEN (amount) ELSE 0 END,
                          CASE WHEN ((status = 2)) THEN (1) ELSE NULL END,
                          CASE WHEN ((status = 3)) THEN (amount) ELSE NULL END
      SEQ_SCAN            orders
```

After:

```
PROJECTION            #0, COALESCE(#1, 0), COALESCE(#2, 0), #3, #4
  PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY   Groups: #0
                          Aggregates: sum_no_overflow(#1) FILTER (WHERE #3),
                                      sum_no_overflow(#1) FILTER (WHERE #4),
                                      count() FILTER (WHERE #5),
                                      avg(#1) FILTER (WHERE #6)
    PROJECTION            customer, amount, status = 0, status = 1, status = 2, status = 3
      SEQ_SCAN            orders
```

On this example (release build, in-memory table, best of 3 on a shared machine): 88 ms -> 65 ms with 8 threads, 0.64 s -> 0.45 s with 1 thread. A single conditional aggregate gains as well: `sum(CASE WHEN c THEN amount ELSE 0 END)` grouped by `customer` runs at 0.92x / 0.85x / 0.77x the instructions of the `CASE` form when 99% / 50% / 1% of the rows match.

### Tests

* `test/optimizer/case_to_filter_aggregate.test`: every rewritten form with the rule disabled and enabled (same rows), grouped and ungrouped, empty inputs, groups without a matching row, NULL arguments and NULL conditions, conditions that are always true or always false, DECIMAL / HUGEINT / UBIGINT / FLOAT / DOUBLE arguments, `IF()`, a `THEN` that can throw, the plans (including the scan after a filter was dropped), and the interaction with partial aggregate pushdown.
* `test/optimizer/case_to_filter_aggregate_exactness.test`: the shapes in which a naive rewrite is not exact: the grand total of ROLLUP / CUBE / GROUPING SETS over an empty input, `inf` / `nan` / `0.1` / `-0.0` constants, `DOUBLE` columns (also as a constant vector), struct fields and list elements of NOT NULL columns.
* `test/optimizer/case_to_filter_aggregate_guards.test`: one negative test per precondition and results on edge inputs.
* `test/optimizer/case_to_filter_aggregate_statistics.test`: the NOT NULL proof against rows that change after the statistics were read: data-modifying CTEs (`UPDATE`, `INSERT`, upsert), uncommitted inserts / updates / `ALTER TABLE` of the running transaction, a prepared statement executed again after an insert, a transaction that still reads NULLs which another connection has overwritten and checkpointed, table functions, recursive CTEs, outer joins, views and materialized CTEs.

The four files pin plans and are added to the skip list of `test/configs/verify_aggregate_state_export.json`, next to the other aggregate rewrite tests.

### Regression check

Rule disabled vs enabled in the same binary (`SET disabled_optimizers`), TPC-H and TPC-DS at SF1 and SF10 and ClickBench: 1 of 22, 9 of 99 and 0 of 43 plans change. Results are identical on TPC-H and TPC-DS SF1 with 1 and 32 threads. title: Keep the struct column qualifier in index expressions when the table shares the column's name
body:
When a table is named like one of its STRUCT columns, the SQL that DuckDB regenerates for an index on that column no longer binds. With `CREATE TABLE s (s STRUCT(n INT)); CREATE INDEX idx ON s ((s.n::VARCHAR));`, `SELECT sql FROM duckdb_indexes()` (and so `EXPORT DATABASE` and the `reparse_statement` verification) returns `CREATE INDEX idx ON s((CAST(n AS VARCHAR)));`, which fails with a binder error because the struct column reference lost its qualifier.

The cause is `RemoveTableQualificationRecursive` in `CreateIndexInfo::ExpressionsToList`: it walks every column reference in the index expression and strips the leading component whenever it equals the table name, so the struct access `s.n` is treated as a table-qualified column `n`. The transformer only ever adds the table qualifier to a top-level, unqualified column reference (`CREATE INDEX idx ON tbl (col)` is stored as `tbl.col`), while references inside expressions are stored exactly as written.

This PR inverts only that step: the qualifier is removed from a top-level two-component reference whose first component is the table name, and expressions are left untouched. Verified with a new sqllogictest that round-trips the regenerated statement, also under `test/configs/verify_statement_to_string.json`, plus `test/sql/index/*`, `test/sql/export/*` and `sqlite_master.test`.

title: Add `variant_value` scalar function
body:
Closes https://github.com/duckdblabs/duckdb-internal/issues/11981

Adds `variant_value`, the VARIANT counterpart of `json_value`. It returns the scalar value at a path or array index of a VARIANT.

```sql
SELECT variant_value({'a': 42, 'b': [1, 2]}::VARIANT, 'a');         -- 42
SELECT variant_value({'a': 42, 'b': [1, 2]}::VARIANT, 'b');         -- NULL, not a scalar
SELECT variant_value({'a': 42, 'b': 'duck'}::VARIANT, ['b', 'a']);  -- [duck, 42]
SELECT variant_value([10, 20, 30]::VARIANT, -1);                    -- 30
```

### Behavior
- Overloads: `(VARIANT, VARCHAR) -> VARIANT`, `(VARIANT, VARCHAR[]) -> VARIANT[]` and `(VARIANT, BIGINT) -> VARIANT`
- The result keeps the type of the selected value 
- Returns `NULL` in these cases:
  - the selected value is an OBJECT, ARRAY or VARIANT null
  - the key is missing or the index is out of range
  - a key is used on a non-object, or an index on a non-array
- Indexes are 0-based; negative indexes count from the end
- The path or index must be constant. A `NULL` inside a list of paths is a `Binder Error`
- For now a path is a single object key, and `''` selects the root. JSONPath support is left for a follow-up
- Only VARIANT input is accepted. A string literal is cast to a VARCHAR VARIANT, not parsed as JSON

### Implementation Notes
- `VariantPathFunction` gets an `ExecuteVariant` method for path functions that return a VARIANT. It builds the result with `BuildVariant`, and a filter decides which values are kept; `variant_value` keeps only scalars. Path handling stays inside `VariantPathFunction`
- The index overload has its own bind data since`VariantPathComponent` cannot store negative indexes

### Tests
`test/sql/function/variant/variant_value.test` and `variant_value_shredded.test` cover:
- the cases above
- every scalar type in `test_all_types()`
- shredded objects and arrays
- inputs larger than one vector
- prepared statements

title: Run a lateral join whose right side is a function of the left row directly over the left rows
body:
## The query shape

Unnesting a list that is built from columns of the same row, or a function of a list column, in the `FROM` clause:

```sql
SELECT id, u.v FROM readings CROSS JOIN UNNEST([a, b, c]) AS u(v);          -- columns to rows
SELECT id, u.v FROM readings, UNNEST(list_reverse(l)) AS u(v);              -- a function of a list column
SELECT id, v FROM readings, LATERAL (SELECT unnest([a, b, c]) AS v);        -- the same as a lateral subquery
```

This is the standard way to turn columns into rows (an unpivot written by hand, key / value pairs built with `[{'k': ..., 'v': ...}, ...]`), to explode a transformed list, and what dialect translation produces for `CROSS JOIN UNNEST(ARRAY[...])` and `LATERAL VIEW explode(array(...))`. The right side has no table of its own: what it produces is a function of the left row alone.

## What happens today

The lateral join is decorrelated the general way: the left rows are materialized in a CTE, their distinct correlated columns are computed with a GROUP BY, the right side runs once per distinct key, and the result is joined back to the left rows on the correlated columns:

```
CTE __duckdb_delim
  SEQ_SCAN readings  [a, b, c, sensor]                              ~3,000,000 rows
  HASH_JOIN  INNER; a = a, b = b, c = c                             ~3,000,000 rows
    CTE_SCAN
    INOUT_FUNCTION unnest
      PROJECTION  list_value(a, b, c), a, b, c
        HASH_GROUP_BY  Groups: #0, #1, #2                           ~2,997,201 rows
          CTE_SCAN
```

The correlated columns of such a query are typically close to unique, so the domain is as large as its input and the plan groups, hashes and probes every row once more than needed. The unnest rewriter removes this for one case, `UNNEST(col)` of a single correlated list column that is unnested as it is; an expression over the correlated columns, several correlated columns, and projections or filters around the unnest keep the plan above.

## The change

A new pass, `lateral_row_function`, before the join order:

```
MATERIALIZED_CTE d (P)                                   PROJECTION[d1 columns, R columns]
  INNER[d1.c = R.c, for every key c]             ->        (chain over P, the columns of P passed through)
    CTE_REF d1
    R = chain over AGGREGATE[group by keys](CTE_REF d2)
```

When the chain between the join and the aggregate consists of operators that map every input row on its own (`PROJECTION`, `FILTER`, `UNNEST`) and none of its expressions is volatile, what the chain produces for a key, and the join then pairs with every left row of that key, is what the chain produces from that left row. So the chain runs directly over the left rows, with the left columns passed through its projections, and a projection restores the column layout of the join:

```
PROJECTION  #1, #2
  UNNEST
    PROJECTION  list_value(a, b, c), sensor
      SEQ_SCAN readings  [a, b, c, sensor]
```

This is the plan of the select-list form `SELECT sensor, unnest([a, b, c]) FROM readings`.

The pass has its own optimizer name and can be switched off with `SET disabled_optimizers = 'lateral_row_function'`.

## Preconditions

Anything else keeps the plan:

- a CTE with default materialization and exactly two references: the left rows as a direct child of an INNER comparison join, and the domain below an aggregate that only groups (bare-column groups, one grouping set, no aggregate functions);
- between the join and the aggregate only `PROJECTION`, `FILTER`, `UNNEST`, or the `unnest` table function with one LIST / ARRAY argument, one output column and no ordinality (it is converted to an `UNNEST`); no volatile expression, because the original plan evaluates the chain once per distinct key and the rewritten plan once per row;
- every join condition is `=` or `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` between a column of the left rows and the group of the aggregate that reads the same column, passed up through bare column references;
- every group is joined, or one of the joined columns is a `row_number() OVER ()` over the left rows (the domain that is planned for a correlated column of a nested type), which identifies the left row by itself;
- `=` conditions, under which a NULL key never joins, become `IS NOT NULL` filters on the left rows; a filter between the aggregate and the domain reference must read group columns only, and then moves onto the left rows.
- unless the join is on a `row_number()`, every key has a type in which values that compare equal are identical (integers, DECIMAL, DATE / TIME / TIMESTAMP, UUID, BLOB, ENUM, VARCHAR without a collation, and lists / structs / arrays of those). The join gives every left row the value of its group of equal keys, so with FLOAT / DOUBLE (`0.0` and `-0.0`, NaN), INTERVAL, collated strings and other types the rewritten plan could read a different value than the join does - in the chain, in a filter below the domain, or above the join - and the plan is kept;
- the CTE definition has no volatile expression and no DML, and the join is not inside a recursive CTE: the definition moves to the place of the join, and inside a recursion it would be computed in every iteration.

Left alone: `WITH ORDINALITY`, `LEFT JOIN LATERAL` (rows without a list element must be kept), a lateral aggregate, window, limit or join against another table, a join on only some of the keys, `AS MATERIALIZED`, volatile expressions, a filter on a non-key column below the domain, keys of the types above (a list of DOUBLE columns, for example), a volatile CTE definition, a join inside a recursive CTE.

The pass is not tied to `UNNEST` or to the decorrelation: a query that joins a CTE with its own `SELECT DISTINCT` keys on all keys has the same shape and is rewritten too (covered by a test).

## Example

```sql
CREATE TABLE readings AS
    SELECT i AS id, i % 1000 AS sensor, (i * 31) % 997 AS a, (i * 17) % 991 AS b, (i * 13) % 983 AS c,
           [i % 5, i % 7, i % 11] AS l
    FROM range(3000000) t(i);
```

Pass switched off and on in the same binary. Instructions are user-mode instructions of a single-threaded run (`perf stat -e instructions:u`, median of 3, including the 0.24 G of process start-up); wall clock is at 8 threads on a shared machine and only indicative.

| query | instructions before | after | wall before | after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `SELECT count(*), sum(id), sum(u.v) FROM readings CROSS JOIN UNNEST([a, b, c]) AS u(v)` | 96.8 G | 1.27 G | 3.1 s | 0.009 s |
| `SELECT sensor, max(u.v), count(*) FROM readings CROSS JOIN UNNEST([a, b, c]) AS u(v) GROUP BY sensor` | 97.1 G | 1.58 G | 3.0 s | 0.014 s |
| `SELECT count(*), sum(id), sum(u.v) FROM readings CROSS JOIN UNNEST(list_reverse(l)) AS u(v)` | 78.5 G | 1.95 G | 1.6 s | 0.013 s |
| `... FROM readings CROSS JOIN UNNEST([{'k': 1, 'x': a}, {'k': 2, 'x': b}, {'k': 3, 'x': c}]) AS u(v) WHERE u.v.x > 500` | 119.1 G | 1.85 G | 2.1 s | 0.015 s |
| `... FROM readings, LATERAL (SELECT unnest([a, b, c]) AS v)` | 5.11 G | 1.28 G | | |
| `... FROM readings, LATERAL (SELECT v FROM (SELECT unnest([a, b, c]) AS v) WHERE v > 500)` | 3.66 G | 1.36 G | | |
| `... FROM readings, UNNEST([a, b]) AS u(v), UNNEST([u.v, c]) AS w(x)` | 55.1 G | 2.53 G | | |
| `WITH d AS (SELECT * FROM readings) ... FROM d JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT a, b, c FROM d) x ON d.a = x.a AND d.b = x.b AND d.c = x.c` | 2.12 G | 0.30 G | | |
| control: `UNNEST(l)` (the case of the unnest rewriter) | 1.05 G | 1.05 G | | |
| control: `SELECT id, unnest([a, b, c]) FROM readings` written by hand | 1.29 G | 1.28 G | 0.009 s | 0.009 s |

One difference is visible besides speed: queries without an `ORDER BY` can return their rows in a different order than before (the order of the left rows instead of the order of the hash join). The values are the same: where the key of the left row could differ from the key of its group, the plan is kept (see the preconditions).

## Regression check

None of the TPC-H and TPC-DS queries has this shape, so the two suites are regression evidence only and the example above carries the case. Both at SF1 and SF10, pass disabled and enabled in the same binary:

- plans: 0 of 121 queries change at either scale factor;
- results at SF1 with 1 and with 16 threads: identical;
- user-mode instructions at 1 thread, median of 3, per query: no query above 1.05x; totals 0.999 (TPC-H SF1), 1.000 (TPC-DS SF1), 1.000 (TPC-H SF10), 0.999 (TPC-DS SF10);
- planning cost: cold `EXPLAIN` of the 99 TPC-DS queries, 0.999x instructions in total.

## Tests

`test/optimizer/lateral_row_function.test` (863 assertions): 37 result cases over a table with duplicate rows, NULL columns, empty and NULL lists and NULL list elements (expression lists, a function of a list column, a list that is NULL for some rows, lateral subqueries with filters on the outer row and on the unnested value, an aggregate and a join above, two chained laterals, an empty left table, struct / VARCHAR / ARRAY lists, `SELECT *`, the bare list column) including the shapes that must stay as they are (`WITH ORDINALITY`, `LEFT JOIN LATERAL`, a lateral aggregate, a lateral over another table, a volatile expression, `AS MATERIALIZED`, a join on only some of the keys, a filter on a non-key column below the `DISTINCT`), keys whose equal values can differ (DOUBLE with `0.0` / `-0.0` and NaN, a filter with `signbit` below the `DISTINCT`, a case-insensitive VARCHAR, INTERVAL), a function of an integer key below the `DISTINCT`, a CTE joined inside a recursive CTE with a sequence in its definition, and a volatile CTE definition; and 27 plan pins for both groups and for the pass disabled by name.

Existing tests that change:

- `test/sql/table_function/range_lateral_threads.test` and `test/sql/json/table/json_table_in_out_threads.test` disable `unnest_rewriter` to keep `LATERAL unnest([i])` planned as a join, so that its pipeline task count can be compared with the per-row table functions. The new pass would rewrite that unnest, so both tests now disable `lateral_row_function` as well. Their expectations are unchanged.

No other expected plan or result changes. The whole fast test suite and `test/optimizer/*`, `test/sql/join/*`, `test/sql/subquery/*`, `test/sql/cte/*`, `test/sql/types/list/*`, `test/sql/types/nested/*`, `test/sql/unnest/*`, `test/sql/table_function/*`, `test/sql/json/*`, `test/sql/tpch/*` and `test/sql/tpcds/*` including the slow tests pass.

Relation to #28102 / #28760: #28102 relaxes the unnest rewriter from a column reference to any non-volatile expression as the `UNNEST` argument. Its diff as of 2026-11-13, built on the same base, rewrites `UNNEST(list_reverse(l))` (78.4 G to 1.94 G instructions on the example table, as here) and leaves the other rows of the table above as they are, including the list of three columns, which is joined back on three keys: 96.8 G with and without it. The two changes do not conflict and do not apply twice to the same join. #28760 / #28639 remove identity projections around the CTEs this pass matches; the plan pins of this test need to be re-run once they land.

title: Filter the outer scan of a correlated EXISTS by a predicate on the outer key only
body:
## The query shape

A correlated `EXISTS` (or correlated `IN`) whose subquery also carries a predicate on the outer key only:

```sql
SELECT ... FROM orders o
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM customers c WHERE c.customer_id = o.customer_id AND o.customer_id > 17000);
```

This is what query generators and hand-written reports produce when a restriction on the outer row is written next to the correlation instead of in the outer `WHERE`: the two places are equivalent for `EXISTS`, and a view or a template often only allows adding conditions inside the subquery. Written in the outer `WHERE`, the predicate is pushed into the scan of `orders`. Written inside the subquery it is not: the outer rows are produced in full and the predicate is only applied to the duplicate-eliminated domain.

## What happens today

The subquery is decorrelated into a materialized CTE of the outer rows with two references: the outer rows on the left side of a MARK join, and the domain of distinct keys below the subquery. The predicate `o.customer_id > 17000` ends up as a filter on the domain reference only. The CTE filter pusher restricts a CTE only when every reference is filtered, so the scan of `orders` stays unfiltered:

```
CTE __duckdb_delim
  SEQ_SCAN orders  [customer_id, amount]                                ~3,000,000 rows
  FILTER  SUBQUERY
    HASH_JOIN  MARK; customer_id IS NOT DISTINCT FROM customer_id
      CTE_SCAN                                                          ~3,000,000 rows
      ... HASH_JOIN INNER customer_id = customer_id
            (GROUP BY over FILTER (#[0.0] > 17000) over CTE_SCAN)
            SEQ_SCAN customers  Filters: customer_id > 17000
```

## The change

A new pass, `semi_join_key_filter_transfer`, between filter pushdown and the CTE filter pusher:

```
SEMI[l = r](CTE_REF c, R)                 ->  SEMI[l = r](FILTER[p(l)](CTE_REF c), R)
FILTER[mark](MARK[l = r](CTE_REF c, R))   ->  FILTER[mark](MARK[l = r](FILTER[p(l)](CTE_REF c), R))
                                              when p(r) is TRUE for every row of R
```

A left row survives a SEMI join, or a MARK join under a filter on the bare mark, only together with a right row whose key equals its own (`=`) or is NULL together with it (`IS NOT DISTINCT FROM`). A predicate that is TRUE for the key of every right row is therefore TRUE for the key of every surviving left row, and filtering the left side by it first removes only rows that the join drops anyway. With the filter on the outer rows' reference every reference of the CTE is filtered, and the existing CTE filter pusher moves the predicate into the CTE definition and filter pushdown moves it into the scan:

```
CTE __duckdb_delim
  SEQ_SCAN orders  [customer_id, amount]  Filters: customer_id > 17000  ~600,000 rows
  FILTER  SUBQUERY
    HASH_JOIN  MARK; customer_id IS NOT DISTINCT FROM customer_id
      FILTER (#[0.0] > 17000)
        CTE_SCAN
      ... (unchanged)
```

The CTE filter pusher gets one addition, limited to the CTEs for which this pass filtered a reference. It restricts a CTE by the disjunction of the filters of its references. When the conjuncts of one reference include all conjuncts of another, as they do here, the larger filter is dropped from the disjunction (`(A AND B) OR A` is `A`), so the scan gets `customer_id > 17000` instead of `(customer_id > 17000 AND ...) OR customer_id > 17000`. Two conjuncts count as the same predicate when they are equal as expressions, and expression equality compares constants by value (`0.0` equals `-0.0`). That is only the same predicate when the constant is compared with a column and not passed to a function such as `signbit`, so every conjunct of the reference that is kept must be a comparison of a bare column with constants (`=`, `<`, ..., `BETWEEN`, `IN` list, `IS [NOT] NULL`, `AND` / `OR` over those); anything else keeps the disjunction. For other CTEs, and with the pass disabled, the CTE filter pusher behaves as before.

The pass has its own optimizer name and can be switched off with `SET disabled_optimizers = 'semi_join_key_filter_transfer'`.

## Preconditions

- The left child of the join is a reference of a materialized CTE (bare or under a filter), not a recurring or correlated reference, and every other reference of that CTE is already filtered. The new filter is then exactly what the CTE filter pusher was missing. Other left sides (for example a plain table scan under an uncorrelated `IN`) are left alone: there the scan is already restricted by join filters at run time and by the value range derived from the join statistics.
- A SEMI comparison join, or a MARK comparison join directly under a filter that has the bare mark as a conjunct. Not ANTI, outer, delim or AsOf joins, and not a mark that is used in any other way (`NOT mark`, under an `OR`, in the select list).
- The join condition is `=` or `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` between two bare columns of the same type.
- Only predicates that are functions of the key value and cannot throw are copied: comparisons with constants, `BETWEEN` with constant bounds, `IN` / `NOT IN` lists of constants, `IS [NOT] NULL`, and `AND` / `OR` over those.
- "Every right row satisfies it" is established by following the right key column down through filters, table filters of a scan (not the optional ones), column-reference projections, the groups of an aggregate with a single grouping set, the preserved side of joins and the equalities of INNER joins. The NULL-extended side of an outer join, grouping sets, set operations and CTE references end the search.
- `IS NOT NULL` is not copied across `=` (the join drops NULL keys anyway), and a predicate that the left side already has is skipped.

## Example

```sql
CREATE TABLE orders AS
    SELECT i AS order_id, (i * 7919) % 20000 AS customer_id, DATE '2024-01-01' + (i % 365)::INTEGER AS order_date,
           ((i % 1000) / 10.0)::DECIMAL(10,1) AS amount, 'note ' || (i % 100000) AS note,
           i % 7 AS status, i % 13 AS channel, i % 101 AS store_id
    FROM range(30000000) t(i);
CREATE TABLE customers AS SELECT i AS customer_id, 'customer ' || i AS name, i % 50 AS region FROM range(18000) t(i);

SELECT status, channel, count(*), sum(amount), max(note), min(order_date), max(store_id)
FROM orders o
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM customers c WHERE c.customer_id = o.customer_id AND <predicate on o.customer_id>)
GROUP BY status, channel;
```

Pass switched off and on in the same binary. Instructions are user-mode instructions of a single-threaded run (`perf stat -e instructions:u`, median of 3, including the 0.24 G of process start-up); wall clock is at 8 threads on a shared machine and only indicative.

| predicate inside the subquery | instructions before | after | wall before | after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `o.customer_id > 17000` (15 % of the rows pass it, 5 % have a match) | 13.5 G | 7.6 G | 0.13 s | 0.07 s |
| `o.customer_id BETWEEN 100 AND 300 AND c.region < 25` | 13.1 G | 4.5 G | 0.13 s | 0.04 s |
| `o.customer_id > 100000` (no row can match) | 9.4 G | 0.26 G | 0.07 s | 0.005 s |
| control: `o.customer_id > 17000` written in the outer `WHERE` | 5.9 G | 5.9 G | 0.05 s | 0.05 s |

The control shows what is left on the table: with the predicate in the outer `WHERE` the subquery is deliminated into a plain semi join. The pass does not rewrite the query into that form, it only stops the scan from producing rows that cannot match.

A correlated `IN` with two join conditions, on a 3,000,000 row version of the same table (`o.store_id IN (SELECT c.region FROM customers c WHERE c.customer_id = o.customer_id AND o.customer_id > 17000)`), goes from 0.93 G to 0.53 G instructions and from 0.038 s to 0.008 s.

## Regression check

None of the TPC-H and TPC-DS queries has this shape, so the two suites are regression evidence only and the example above carries the case. Both at SF1 and SF10, pass disabled and enabled in the same binary:

- plans: 0 of 121 queries change at either scale factor;
- results at SF1 with 1 and with 16 threads: identical;
- user-mode instructions at 1 thread, median of 3, per query: no query above 1.05x; totals 0.999 (TPC-H SF1), 0.999 (TPC-DS SF1), 1.000 (TPC-H SF10), 1.000 (TPC-DS SF10);
- planning cost: cold `EXPLAIN` of the 99 TPC-DS queries, 0.999x instructions in total.

On the shapes the pass does not apply to (an `EXISTS` without an outer-only predicate, the predicate written in the outer `WHERE`) plans and instruction counts are unchanged.

## Tests

title: Fold comparisons with a column that holds only NULLs during statistics propagation
body:
## The query shape

A filter or a join condition that compares a column that holds only NULLs with another column or expression:

```sql
SELECT ... FROM cast_member c JOIN person p ON p.legacy_id = c.person_id;   -- legacy_id was never filled in
SELECT ... FROM cast_member WHERE note_id <> person_id;                     -- note_id is NULL in every row
```

Columns like this are common in real schemas: an optional foreign key that a migration added and nothing populates yet, a column kept for compatibility, a wide generated table of which only some columns are used. Queries written by people or generated by tools join and filter on them regardless. Such a comparison is NULL for every row, so the filter keeps nothing and the join matches nothing, but today the plan still scans, builds and probes.

## What happens today

Statistics propagation prunes a comparison by the value ranges of its two operands. A column that holds only NULLs has no range, so `PropagateComparison` returns "no pruning possible". The fact that the column has no valid value is used in two places only: `x IS [NOT] NULL` is folded, and a comparison with a constant that was pushed into a scan is pruned by the table filter. A comparison between two columns, or between a column and an expression, is kept.

## The change

During statistics propagation, when the statistics of an operand say that it can be NULL and cannot be anything else, the comparison is replaced by a `NULL::BOOLEAN` constant:

| expression | folded when |
|---|---|
| `=`, `<>`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` | either operand holds only NULLs |
| `x BETWEEN a AND b` | `x` holds only NULLs |
| `x [NOT] IN (...)` | `x` holds only NULLs |
| a BOOLEAN function with default NULL handling (`LIKE`, `contains`, ...) | an argument holds only NULLs |

What follows from the NULL constant is the existing machinery: a filter becomes an empty result; for a join condition `HandleJoinNeverMatches` is used, so INNER / SEMI joins become an empty result, LEFT / RIGHT joins keep the preserved side and get an empty other side, ANTI joins keep their left side, and FULL / MARK / SINGLE joins are left as they are.

One addition outside the propagator: the early filter-statistics pass (`FilterStatisticsOptimizer`, which runs before the join order) so far only runs for plans with a multi-table filter. It now also runs when a filter or join condition reads a scanned column that holds only NULLs, so that the empty result is known before the join order is chosen and the remaining joins are not ordered around a join that cannot match. The check costs one statistics lookup per compared scan column.

There is no new optimizer switch: this is part of `statistics_propagation` and is switched off with it.

## Preconditions

- Not `IS [NOT] DISTINCT FROM` (NULLs compare equal there). Where the existing simplification turns `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` into `=` because the other side has no NULLs, the `=` is folded.
- Not a bound of a `BETWEEN`: with a NULL bound the result is FALSE or NULL, which is not a constant.
- Not `COALESCE`, `CASE`, `OR`, `IS NULL`: these are not NULL for a NULL operand.
- No operand may throw, be volatile or sit behind an expression barrier (`CAST(varchar_col AS DOUBLE)`, `random()`): removing the comparison would remove the error or the side effect. `TRY_CAST`, casts that cannot fail and arithmetic that the statistics prove cannot overflow are fine.
- The statistics must say "has NULLs, has no valid value". Statistics of an empty input (neither) are left alone, so plans over empty tables do not change.

The claim "no valid value" is the one that the `IS NULL` folding and the table filter pruning already rely on. The cases in which it could be stale each have a test:

| case | behaviour |
|---|---|
| one non-NULL value among 10,000 rows | not folded, the row is found |
| `UPDATE` to a value and back to NULL | not folded while the value is there, the row is found; 0 rows after |
| committed append of a non-NULL value | not folded |
| transaction-local append (one row, and several row groups) and transaction-local update | the local statistics are merged: not folded, the local row is found |
| transaction-local append of NULLs only | 0 rows |
| another connection's uncommitted append | not visible to this connection: 0 rows here, 1 row in the other connection |
| a snapshot opened before another connection commits a non-NULL value | the result of the snapshot: 0 rows before and after the commit, 1 row in the next transaction |
| a snapshot that still sees a row another connection deleted, plus a `CHECKPOINT` | the row is not dropped while a snapshot sees it: 1 row |
| a snapshot that still sees a value another connection updated to NULL (one row, and every row of the column) | the rows of the snapshot |
| every row updated to NULL, then `CHECKPOINT` | the statistics know that the column holds only NULLs: folded; not folded again after one row is updated to a value |
| a prepared statement, the table changed between two `EXECUTE` | 0 rows, then 1 row |
| `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN`, then `UPDATE` | 0 rows, then all rows |

Outside the test file, 33 queries were compared with and without statistics propagation on a database that was checkpointed and reopened, on Parquet files (one file, lists of files in either order, an empty file first), through `UNION ALL`, `VALUES`, materialized CTEs, windows, aggregates, the NULL-extended side of outer joins, `unnest`, `CASE`, `COALESCE`, structs and lists: all results are identical.

One difference a user can observe besides speed: an error that another conjunct or operator of the pruned plan would have raised is not raised, because that part of the plan no longer runs. This is the behaviour of the empty results that statistics propagation already derives from value ranges; the test file pins one case of each.

## Example

```sql
CREATE TABLE person AS SELECT i AS id, 'person ' || i AS name, NULL::BIGINT AS legacy_id FROM range(2000000) t(i);
CREATE TABLE movie AS SELECT i AS id, 'movie ' || i AS title, 1950 + i % 70 AS year FROM range(500000) t(i);
CREATE TABLE note AS SELECT i AS id, 'note ' || i AS text FROM range(1000) t(i);
CREATE TABLE cast_member AS
    SELECT i AS id, (i * 7919) % 2000000 AS person_id, (i * 104729) % 500000 AS movie_id,
           i % 12 AS role_id, NULL::BIGINT AS note_id
    FROM range(20000000) t(i);

SELECT m.year, count(*)
FROM cast_member c JOIN movie m ON m.id = c.movie_id JOIN person p ON p.legacy_id = c.person_id
GROUP BY m.year;
```

Before:

```
PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY  Groups: #0; Aggregates: count_star()
  HASH_JOIN  INNER; movie_id = id                          ~16,468,003 rows
    HASH_JOIN  INNER; person_id = legacy_id                ~17,701,127 rows
      SEQ_SCAN cast_member  [movie_id, person_id]          ~20,000,000 rows
      SEQ_SCAN person  [legacy_id]                         ~2,000,000 rows
    SEQ_SCAN movie  [id, year]                             ~500,000 rows
```

After:

```
HASH_GROUP_BY  Groups: #0; Aggregates: count_star()
  PROJECTION  year
    EMPTY_RESULT
```

A LEFT join keeps its left side and no longer reads the other table:

```
-- SELECT count(*), count(p.id) FROM cast_member c LEFT JOIN person p ON p.legacy_id = c.person_id;
HASH_JOIN  LEFT; person_id = legacy_id
  SEQ_SCAN cast_member  [person_id]
  EMPTY_RESULT
```

Measured on the example database with the change switched off and on in the same binary. Instructions are user-mode instructions of a single-threaded run (`perf stat -e instructions:u`, median of 3) minus the 237 M of a `SELECT 1` on the same database; wall clock is at 8 threads on a shared machine and only indicative.

| query | instructions before | after | wall before | after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| the three-table join above | 163 M | 15 M | 0.008 s | 0.001 s |
| `... cast_member c JOIN person p ON p.id = c.person_id JOIN movie m ON m.id = c.movie_id JOIN note n ON n.id = c.note_id GROUP BY n.text` | 495 M | 15 M | 0.015 s | 0.001 s |
| `... cast_member c JOIN cast_member c2 ON c.movie_id = c2.movie_id JOIN person p ON p.id = c.person_id JOIN person p2 ON p2.legacy_id = c2.person_id WHERE p.name LIKE 'person 1%'` | 4,881 M | 17 M | 0.075 s | 0.001 s |
| `SELECT role_id, count(*) FROM cast_member WHERE note_id <> person_id GROUP BY role_id` | 613 M | 12 M | 0.005 s | < 0.001 s |
| the LEFT join above | 432 M | 382 M | 0.004 s | 0.003 s |

The executor already stops a hash join early when its build side has no valid key, which is why the first numbers are small in absolute terms. What the plan-level pruning adds is everything the executor cannot skip: the scan and filter of the column, the joins that feed the build side of a join whose probe side is the NULL column (third row), and a join order that is no longer chosen around a join that cannot match.

## Regression check

TPC-H and TPC-DS at SF1 and SF10, change switched off and on in the same binary:

- plans: 0 of 121 queries change at either scale factor;
- results at SF1 with 1 and with 16 threads: identical (one TPC-DS query that divides two floating-point aggregates varies in the last digit between runs of the same configuration at 16 threads; it is identical at 1 thread);
- user-mode instructions at 1 thread, median of 3, per query: no query above 1.05x; totals 1.001 (TPC-H SF1), 1.000 (TPC-DS SF1), 0.999 (TPC-H SF10), 1.000 (TPC-DS SF10);
- planning cost of the additional check: cold `EXPLAIN` of the 99 TPC-DS queries, 1.0004x instructions in total (largest single query 1.010x); TPC-H 0.999x.

## Tests

`test/optimizer/statistics/statistics_all_null_operand.test` (301 assertions): the six comparisons between two columns in filters, `BETWEEN`, `[NOT] IN`, `LIKE` / `NOT LIKE` / `contains`, the NULL constant in a projection, INNER joins with and without casts, a five-way join that is gone before the join order, one condition of several, SEMI, and LEFT / RIGHT / FULL / ANTI / MARK / SINGLE joins with their results; a negative case for every precondition above (`IS [NOT] DISTINCT FROM`, a `BETWEEN` bound, `COALESCE`, `OR`, `CASE`, casts that can throw, which keep the comparison in the plan, `TRY_CAST`, arithmetic, `random()`, an empty table); the statistics cases of the table above with two connections; views, aggregates, outer joins and nested types above the column; and the plans with `statistics_propagation` disabled.

Existing tests that change:

- `test/sql/join/iejoin/iejoin_issue_6861.test` runs an IE join over a table whose column was updated to NULL in every row and pins `IE_JOIN` in the plan. In the default in-memory run the statistics still hold the old values, so nothing changes there; under the test configs that run on persistent storage (and in memory after a `CHECKPOINT`) the statistics know that the column holds only NULLs and the comparison is folded to an empty result. The test is about executing the join over all-NULL input, so it now disables `statistics_propagation` for those queries, which keeps the join in the plan under every config. Its results are unchanged.

No other expected plan or result changes. The whole fast test suite and `test/optimizer/*`, `test/sql/join/*`, `test/sql/subquery/*`, `test/sql/cte/*`, `test/sql/filter/*`, `test/sql/transactions/*`, `test/sql/update/*`, `test/sql/delete/*`, `test/sql/types/list/*`, `test/sql/unnest/*`, `test/sql/tpch/*` and `test/sql/tpcds/*` including the slow tests pass. The new test is added to `test/configs/stats_dependent_tests.json`, the list of tests that are skipped when the optimizer is disabled because they depend on statistics; it passes under the other test configs. The whole test suite was also run under each config of `make test_configs`.
