title: Bound a table scan's estimate by the rows of the row groups its filters cannot skip
body:
## What this applies to

Filters on a column whose values are stored in runs: an append-ordered timestamp or date, an auto-incremented id, a table loaded sorted or partition by partition. "The last day of an event log", "orders of one quarter" or "ids above a watermark" select a contiguous slice of such a table, and the scan already skips every row group outside that slice through its zonemaps (the per-row-group min/max).

The planner does not use that information. A range filter is estimated from the table-level statistics with the default selectivity of 0.2 as its floor, so a filter that keeps 0.1 % of an append-ordered table is planned as if it kept 20 %. The scan then looks two orders of magnitude larger than it is, and the join order and the build side are chosen for the wrong sizes.

## What changes

The estimate of a DuckDB table scan with table filters is bounded by the rows of the row groups whose zonemaps can satisfy all of its filters. The row groups come from the existing `get_partition_stats` callback (what the row group pruner and the `count(*)` statistics shortcut already read at plan time), and the per-row-group check is `ExpressionFilter::CheckExpressionStatistics`, the check the scan itself uses to skip a row group. This part is a count, not an estimate: rows of row groups the scan will skip are not returned.

On top of that, a row group that a range filter cuts (it cannot be skipped, but only part of its `[min, max]` lies inside the range) counts for the covered share of its own `[min, max]`. That is an interpolation, so it is only applied where the zonemaps show that the column is stored in runs:

* the row group covers at most half of the span of the column over the table (two row groups that each cover more than half overlap), and
* the spans of all row groups add up to at most twice the span of the column. The row groups of a sorted column tile its span once; at two, a value lies in two row groups on average and a narrow `[min, max]` is not a slice of a sorted order.

Several range filters on one row group combine the way their estimates over the table do: the smallest share counts.

Everywhere else a row group that cannot be skipped counts whole, and the estimate is what it was. In particular a column that is not clustered is untouched: every row group spans the whole range, nothing is skipped, nothing is interpolated. A row group that holds a single value is not cut by a range and counts whole.

The result only ever lowers an estimate: it is combined with the existing estimate by `min`. Row groups are counted with the rows the planning transaction can see, so rows it has deleted are not counted and rows deleted by a transaction it cannot see still are.

### Relation to #28341

#28341 interpolates integer ranges over the table-level `[min, max]` and deliberately keeps the default selectivity as the floor of that interpolation (`integer_range_selectivity_floor.test`: "narrow ranges keep the 0.2 floor"). This PR keeps the same floor wherever it interpolates: a cut row group counts for `max(0.2, covered share)` of its rows. The estimate goes below 20 % of the table only through row groups that are skipped whole, which are counted from the zonemaps rather than interpolated. For a table of a single row group, or a column that is not stored in runs, nothing changes and the tests of #28341 pass unchanged.

### Relation to #28664

#28664 estimates the selectivity of a scan's filters on a row sample and inserts that estimate at the same place, directly before `ApplyFilterEstimate`. The two are complementary: a sample estimates any filter on any layout, the zonemaps give a count for the rows a scan cannot return. Both are combined with the existing estimate by `min`, so they compose in either order; whichever lands second rebases those few lines.

### Preconditions

* a DuckDB table scan (`get_partition_stats` with row group statistics); other sources keep their estimate;
* at least one non-optional table filter without parameters on a regular column (not the row id, not a generated column); optional filters do not restrict the result and are ignored;
* skipping applies to every filter and type the zonemap check understands (comparisons, `IN`, `IS NULL`, string prefixes, ...); the interpolation applies to `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` and their conjunctions on numeric, DECIMAL, DATE and TIMESTAMP columns;
* the table has at most 16,384 row groups (2 billion rows at the default row group size). A larger table keeps its estimate: checking only some of its row groups would not give a bound, because the row groups that are not checked can hold all of the matching rows;
* the estimate is above one row. The walk also stops as soon as the rows counted so far reach the current estimate, since the bound can no longer improve on it.

No table data is read. For a table that was just opened, the zonemaps of the filtered columns are loaded at plan time instead of at the start of the scan, which needs them anyway.

The rule has its own `OptimizerType`, `scan_selectivity_zonemaps`, so `SET disabled_optimizers = 'scan_selectivity_zonemaps'` restores the previous estimates.

## Example

```sql
-- an event log appended in time order: one event per second for about 579 days
CREATE TABLE events AS
    SELECT TIMESTAMP '2024-01-01' + INTERVAL (range) SECOND AS ts, (range * 7919) % 2000000 AS user_id, range % 100 AS kind
    FROM range(50000000);
CREATE TABLE users AS SELECT range AS user_id, 'user ' || range AS name, range % 50 AS country FROM range(2000000);

SELECT u.country, count(*)
FROM events e JOIN users u ON e.user_id = u.user_id
WHERE e.ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-08-01'
GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY ALL LIMIT 3;
```

The filter keeps 60,800 of 50,000,000 events.

| | estimated rows of the `events` scan | actual | hash join |
|---|---|---|---|
| before | 10,000,000 | 60,800 | builds on `users` (2,000,000 rows), probes with `events` |
| after | 60,800 | 60,800 | builds on the filtered `events` (60,800 rows), probes `users` behind a runtime filter on `user_id` |

Timings of the query (release build, in-memory, best of 3, shared machine):

| threads | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.052 s | 0.009 s |
| 8 | 0.015 s | 0.005 s |

Planning cost. The work per plan is limited to the row groups of one table of at most 16,384 row groups, and the limit is tested on the row group count before any row group is loaded or collected (`DataTable::GetRowGroupCountWithoutLoading`, a small accessor this PR adds). `EXPLAIN` time at 1 thread with the zonemaps in memory, rule off / on, on tables of 2,048-row row groups with a sorted `id`:

| row groups | `id = <constant>` | `id < 100000` |
|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | 0.47 / 0.81 ms (estimate 2 rows) | 0.50 / 0.93 ms |
| 16,000 | 0.50 / 0.43 ms (estimate 1 row, not read) | 0.56 / 8.9 ms |
| 100,000 | 0.59 / 0.63 ms (above the limit) | 0.54 / 0.49 ms (above the limit) |

The 16,000-row-group range query is the worst case under the limit: about 0.5 µs per row group and filter, the same check the scan makes for each row group when it runs. The first plan after opening a database also loads the zonemaps of the filtered columns (63 ms for 16,000 row groups, 8 ms for a 60M-row table with 489 row groups and three filters), which the scan otherwise does at its start.

## Regression check

Rule disabled vs enabled in the same binary (`disabled_optimizers`), one process per query and arm.

* TPC-H SF1 / SF10 and TPC-DS SF1 / SF10 as generated (not stored in date order): EXPLAIN output, including every estimate, is identical with the rule on and off for all queries. JOB: 13 of 113 queries get a lower estimate for one scan (a string filter on a column that happens to be clustered skips row groups); no plan shape changes.
* Results at 1, 8 and 64 threads on TPC-H SF1 / SF10 and TPC-DS SF1 / SF10 are the same with the rule on and off (one TPC-DS query that divides DOUBLE aggregates differs in the last digit between thread counts, with and without the rule).
* User-mode instructions at 1 thread (`perf stat -e instructions:u`, median of 3), geometric mean on / off: TPC-H SF1 0.999, SF10 0.999; TPC-DS SF1 1.000, SF10 0.999; JOB 0.997. No query is above 1.05x: two first-pass readings of 1.05 and 1.06, both on queries whose EXPLAIN output is identical in both arms, were re-run with 11 and 31 repetitions and came out at 1.02 and 0.99.
* The same benchmark stored in runs (TPC-H SF10 with `lineitem` in ship date order and `orders` in order date order, as an append-by-time load would produce): the estimates of the date-range scans go from a q-error of 5.2 to 16.0 down to 1.00 to 1.02 (one quarter of orders: 3,000,000 estimated before, 574,903 after, 573,671 actual; one month of line items: 11,997,210 before, 757,760 after, 749,223 actual). 8 of 22 queries get different estimates, 3 plans change, results are identical at 1, 8 and 64 threads; instructions geometric mean 0.978, best 0.63, worst 1.02.

## Tests

* `test/optimizer/statistics/scan_selectivity_zonemaps.test`: ranges on a sorted key and a clustered date (exact to the row group), the default-selectivity floor of a cut row group, a conjunction across two columns that only the row groups refute, and one negative case per precondition: a permuted column, a dense skewed column that is not stored in runs, a sparse column whose row groups overlap (covered twice or more), row groups that hold a single value; results with the rule on and off; and the rows a transaction can see: its own inserts, an uncommitted update (the zonemap of its row group widens at once), its own deletes, a rollback, and a transaction that started before another connection committed a delete (it still sees the rows, and they are still counted).
* `test/optimizer/statistics/scan_selectivity_zonemaps_guards.test`: one row group selected exactly for INTEGER, a nullable column, `IS NULL`, VARCHAR, DECIMAL and TIMESTAMP; unchanged EXPLAIN output for a scan without filters, a Parquet scan, a filter no zonemap refutes, a range on an unclustered column, a row id filter and an empty table; a filter the table statistics refute keeps its 0 rows; a join whose build side follows the estimate; a table that was just attached.
* `test/optimizer/statistics/scan_selectivity_zonemaps_row_group_limit.test_slow`: a table of 16,000 row groups (bounded) and one of 16,386 whose matching rows are in every other row group (keeps its estimate).

No existing test expectation changes.

title: Remove DISTINCT / GROUP BY without aggregates over an input that is already distinct
body:
`SELECT DISTINCT` is often written defensively, or generated by a tool, on top of something that cannot contain duplicates in the first place: the columns include the primary key of the table, the input is a `GROUP BY` on the same columns, a join against the key of a lookup table sits in between, or the input of an `INTERSECT` / `EXCEPT` is itself a `DISTINCT`. DuckDB plans every `DISTINCT` (and every `GROUP BY` without aggregate functions) as a hash aggregate over all input rows, also when the result is known to be the input.

This PR adds an optimizer, `redundant_distinct`, that removes such an aggregate when its input provably has at most one row per value of the group columns. The aggregate is replaced by a projection of the groups under the same table index, so nothing above it has to be rebound. It runs before join ordering.

The proof is structural, in a small helper (`Distinctness::IsDistinctOn`):

* sources: the groups of an aggregate with a single grouping set, and the `PRIMARY KEY` / `UNIQUE NOT NULL` constraints of a scanned table (through the existing `ApplyFunctionalDependencies::GetUniqueColumnCombinations`);
* these stay distinct through operators that never duplicate a row: filters, limits, orderings, samples, windows, projections (plain column references only), the left side of SEMI / ANTI / MARK / SINGLE joins, and a side of an INNER join (the left side of a LEFT join) whose other side is distinct on the columns of the join's equality conditions.

Statistics (distinct counts) are estimates and are never used.

### Preconditions

The aggregate is removed only if

* it has no aggregate functions and no `GROUPING` functions, and one grouping set that contains all groups;
* every group is a plain column reference;
* some set of columns that is proven distinct for the input is contained in the groups.

Things that do not prove anything, each pinned by a test: a nullable `UNIQUE` column (several NULLs are one group), part of a composite key, an expression or cast of a key, a second grouping set, a LEFT join against a side that is not distinct on the join key (and the null-extended side of any outer join), an inequality or an expression as the only join condition, an AsOf join, a cross product, a `UNION ALL`, a table function.

`SET disabled_optimizers = 'redundant_distinct'` switches it off.

### Example

```sql
CREATE TABLE customers(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, country INTEGER, segment INTEGER);
INSERT INTO customers SELECT i, i % 50, i % 7 FROM range(2000000) t(i);
CREATE TABLE orders(id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER, amount INTEGER);
INSERT INTO orders SELECT i, (i * 7919) % 2000000, i % 97 FROM range(20000000) t(i);
CREATE TABLE visits AS SELECT (i * 31) % 3000000 AS customer_id, i % 365 AS day FROM range(30000000) t(i);

SELECT DISTINCT o.id, o.amount FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE c.country < 25;
```

`orders.id` is a key, and the join against the key of `customers` does not duplicate orders. Before:

```
AGGREGATE Groups: id, amount                                   ~8,803,200 rows
  COMPARISON_JOIN Join Type: INNER; Conditions: customer_id = id
    SEQ_SCAN orders
    SEQ_SCAN customers Filters: country < 25
```

After:

```
PROJECTION Expressions: id, amount
  COMPARISON_JOIN Join Type: INNER; Conditions: customer_id = id
    SEQ_SCAN orders
    SEQ_SCAN customers Filters: country < 25
```

User-mode instructions at one thread (`perf stat -e instructions:u`, median of 3, release build, `redundant_distinct` disabled vs. enabled in the same binary; the queries are wrapped in `SELECT count(*) FROM (...)`):

| query | disabled | enabled | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| the query above | 5.02e9 | 2.76e9 | 0.55 |
| `SELECT DISTINCT id, country, segment FROM customers` | 7.29e8 | 2.93e8 | 0.40 |
| `SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM (SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS n FROM visits GROUP BY customer_id) WHERE n > 5` | 3.76e9 | 3.28e9 | 0.87 |
| `SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM visits INTERSECT SELECT id FROM customers WHERE country < 25` | 2.76e9 | 2.60e9 | 0.94 |

### Regression check

Disabled vs. enabled in the same binary on TPC-H and TPC-DS (SF1 and SF10, with and without declared keys), JOB and ClickBench: the results are identical at 1 and 32 threads (TPC-H / TPC-DS SF1, with and without keys). title: Generate join filters for RIGHT ANTI joins
body:
An anti join whose preserved side is small and whose other side is large ("accounts in this region that have no event", `small EXCEPT big`, an `ANTI JOIN` against a fact table) is flipped by the build side optimizer into a RIGHT ANTI join: the small side is built, the large side probes. The probe rows of a RIGHT ANTI join are never emitted, they only mark build rows as matched, and the join returns the build rows that were not marked. A probe row whose key does not occur on the build side cannot mark anything, so it does not have to reach the join at all. That is exactly the situation join filter pushdown exists for, and it already handles RIGHT SEMI joins this way, but `JoinFilterPushdownUtil::JoinTypeIsSupported` rejected RIGHT ANTI together with ANTI ("FIXME: anti/right_anti - we could do this, but need to invert the join conditions"). The inversion is only needed for a plain ANTI join, whose unmatched probe rows are the result. For RIGHT ANTI the build keys can be pushed into the probe side as they are.

This PR makes RIGHT ANTI a supported join type for join filters:

`JOIN_FILTER_PUSHDOWN` generates the filters (min/max, IN list, bloom filter, as for any other join) for RIGHT ANTI comparison joins, including the filters that are pushed into a materialized CTE on the probe side.

Plain ANTI joins stay unsupported. The choice of the build side is not changed: `BUILD_SIDE_PROBE_SIDE` does not give RIGHT ANTI the dynamic filter bonus it gives RIGHT SEMI. An ANTI join with a small filtered preserved side is flipped by the size comparison already, and I found no case in which the bonus alone decides the orientation (it needs a preserved side that is at least 64 times smaller in rows than the scan on the other side and still more expensive to build). Nothing changes in the executor: the hash join already publishes its filters independently of the join type.

### Preconditions

* the join is a RIGHT ANTI comparison join (i.e. an ANTI join that the build side optimizer flipped);
* everything `JOIN_FILTER_PUSHDOWN` requires for the other join types: the probe-side key expressions are not volatile, and the filter is only pushed through operators and into scans that accept it.

The behavior has its own optimizer type: `SET disabled_optimizers = 'join_filter_right_anti'` restores the previous plans (`'join_filter_pushdown'` disables these filters together with all other join filters).

### Example

```sql
CREATE TABLE accounts AS SELECT i AS id, i % 50 AS region, i % 7 AS tier FROM range(2000000) t(i);
CREATE TABLE events AS SELECT (i * 31) % 3000000 AS account_id, i % 365 AS day, i % 97 AS amount FROM range(60000000) t(i);

SELECT count(*) FROM accounts a ANTI JOIN events e ON a.id = e.account_id WHERE a.region = 7 AND a.tier = 3;
```

`EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, before:

```
HASH_JOIN    Join Type: RIGHT_ANTI; Conditions: account_id = id
  TABLE_SCAN events    Projections: account_id                                             60,000,000 rows
  TABLE_SCAN accounts  Filters: region = 7, tier = 3                                            5,714 rows
```

After:

```
HASH_JOIN    Join Type: RIGHT_ANTI; Conditions: account_id = id
  TABLE_SCAN events    Projections: account_id; Dynamic Filters: optional: account_id IN PRF(id)  114,280 rows
  TABLE_SCAN accounts  Filters: region = 7, tier = 3                                               5,714 rows
```

User-mode instructions at one thread (`perf stat -e instructions:u`, median of 3, release build, `join_filter_right_anti` disabled vs. enabled in the same binary):

| query | disabled | enabled | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ANTI JOIN` (above) | 3.21e9 | 2.14e9 | 0.67 |
| `SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE region = 7 AND tier = 3 EXCEPT SELECT account_id FROM events` | 3.21e9 | 2.15e9 | 0.67 |

A `NOT EXISTS` over the same tables does not change: it is decorrelated into a different plan that already restricts the scan of `events`.

### Regression check

Disabled vs. enabled in the same binary on TPC-H and TPC-DS (SF1 and SF10), JOB and ClickBench: the results are identical at 1 and 32 threads (TPC-H / TPC-DS SF1), and no `EXPLAIN` plan changes (join filters are not part of the plan text, and no join changes sides). 3 of the 121 TPC-H / TPC-DS queries have a RIGHT ANTI join; their instructions at one thread are between 0.97x and 1.02x. There is none in JOB or ClickBench.

### Tests

`test/optimizer/pushdown/join_filter_pushdown_right_anti.test` (new): `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` pins that the probe scan of a RIGHT ANTI join gets `Dynamic Filters` (also next to an inequality between the two sides), that a plain ANTI join, a volatile probe key, `disabled_optimizers = 'join_filter_right_anti'` and `'join_filter_pushdown'` give none, and results for NULL keys on either side with `=` and `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM`, `NOT IN`, duplicate build keys, two equality keys, VARCHAR keys, an empty probe side, an empty build side, an anti join below an outer join, over an aggregate, over a materialized CTE (one consumer, two anti join consumers whose filters are combined, and an anti join next to an unfiltered consumer), `EXCEPT`, and inside a recursive CTE.

No existing expected plan changes. The tests in `test/optimizer`, `test/sql/join`, `test/sql/subquery`, `test/sql/aggregate`, `test/sql/optimizer`, `test/sql/cte`, `test/sql/setops`, `test/sql/sql_export` and the TPC-H / TPC-DS SF1 answer tests pass, `test/optimizer` and `test/sql/subquery` also with `debug_verify_column_bindings` enabled.

#28732 converts more `NOT EXISTS` / `NOT IN` joins into ANTI joins before join ordering, which produces more RIGHT ANTI joins for this change to act on.

This PR is independent of the other optimizer PRs I am opening next to it (#28786); they add entries to `OptimizerType` as well, so they will conflict textually with each other.

title: Partial aggregate pushdown: pre-aggregate below the join when the aggregate already exports its state (ROLLUP / CUBE / GROUPING SETS over a join)
body:
## What this changes

`PartialAggregatePushdown` pre-aggregates the aggregate side of a join by the join key when the query groups by columns of the other side (the one-sided eager group-by). It does this for a plain `GROUP BY`, but never for `GROUP BY ROLLUP (...)`, `CUBE (...)` or cascadable `GROUPING SETS (...)` over the same join.

The reason is an interaction of two passes. The grouping sets optimizer turns a ROLLUP into a cascade: the finest level aggregates the join and exports its aggregate states (`EXPORT_STATE`), and every coarser level combines the states of the level below it (`combine_aggr`). `IsSupportedAggregate` rejects an aggregate that already exports its state (2096a3d233f), because the pushdown would export it a second time and finalize the result, which does not give back the type the cascade expects. So the finest level, the only one that reads the join, is never pushed.

This PR handles that case instead of rejecting it. For an aggregate that already exports its state:

- the lower aggregate (below the join, grouped by the join key) is the exported aggregate as it is. It is not exported a second time.
- the upper aggregate (above the join, the original groups) is `combine_aggr(state)`, as for every other pushed aggregate.
- the final projection passes the combined state on instead of calling `finalize`, because the consumers of the aggregate (the coarser levels of the cascade) expect the state.

The finest level then looks like every other level of the cascade: it combines states. The trigger is the existing one (`PassesCardinalityHeuristic`, `PassesLowerGroupHeuristic`), and the double-eager and owner-outer rewrites still refuse exported aggregates.

Two things come with it:

- An exported aggregate whose update or combine can throw is not pushed below an inner join (see "When it fires").
- A hash aggregate of `combine_aggr` can now spill arena-backed states. `AggregateStateSpilling::TryCreateSpillPlan` needs the state layout of every aggregate, and `combine_aggr` has no state type of its own, so a level that combines states (every coarser level of a cascade, and with this PR the finest one) could not move its states to spillable storage the way the aggregate that exported them can. The spill plan now takes the layout of the aggregate whose states `combine_aggr` accumulates (`ExportAggregateFunction::TryGetCombinedStateLayout`). `combine_aggr` itself does not get a state type callback: that would make it exportable, and the optimizer passes that look at `HasGetStateTypeCallback` would start exporting it.

## Query shape

A grouped aggregate over a fact table joined to one or more dimension tables, grouped by dimension columns with subtotals:

```sql
SELECT d.a, d.b, sum(f.x), avg(f.x), count(*)
FROM fact f JOIN dim d ON f.k = d.k
GROUP BY ROLLUP (d.a, d.b);
```

This is the usual form of a reporting query: totals per product, with subtotals per brand and per category, and a grand total. The fact table has many rows per join key, the groups are wide dimension attributes (names, categories), and the aggregates are sums, counts, averages, minima and maxima of fact columns. Without the pushdown every fact row is joined to its dimension row and then hashed on the wide group columns. With it, the fact rows are aggregated once on the integer join key, and the join and the cascade above it only see one row per key.

It also applies to an aggregate that a query exports itself (`sum(x) EXPORT_STATE` grouped by dimension columns over a join): the states are combined above the join and returned without a `finalize`.

## When it fires

All preconditions of the one-sided pushdown apply unchanged. The aggregate must

- sit directly on an INNER comparison join, or on a LEFT / RIGHT join that preserves the aggregate side, with equality conditions whose aggregate-side keys are column references;
- have no DISTINCT, FILTER or ORDER BY, at most one argument, and a state type (`HasGetStateTypeCallback`);
- take its arguments from one side of the join only, and group by at least one column of the other side, with more group columns than the lower aggregate would have;
- have no argument that can throw below an inner join (#28573);
- new, for an aggregate that already exports its state: not be able to throw in its update or combine below an inner join. The lower aggregate also aggregates the rows the join removes, so `sum` / `avg` over HUGEINT or DECIMAL(38), which add with an overflow check, could fail on rows the query never aggregates. The check is the function's own error mode (`FunctionErrors::CAN_THROW_RUNTIME_ERROR`, what `BoundAggregateExpression::CanThrow` reads), not a list of types. As with throwing arguments, a LEFT / RIGHT join that preserves the aggregate side keeps every row anyway and is still pushed;
- pass the cardinality heuristic (the join keeps at least 70 % of the aggregate side and that side is at least 4x the other side, or the join expands).

The estimate of the new lower aggregate is capped as in #28716.

For a cascade, the grouping sets optimizer only exports aggregates that are combinable and have no destructor, so the aggregates that reach the pushdown this way are `sum`, `count`, `count(*)`, `avg`, `min`, `max`, `any_value` / `first` / `last`, `bool_and` / `bool_or`, `bit_and` / `bit_or` / `bit_xor`, `product` and `approx_count_distinct`. Below an inner join the variants marked as able to throw stay above the join: `sum` and `avg` over HUGEINT and DECIMAL(38), `skewness`, `kurtosis`. DISTINCT and ordered aggregates are not part of a cascade and stay where they are.

The plain `GROUP BY` path of the pass is not changed by this PR. It does not have the new check, so `sum(HUGEINT)` grouped by dimension columns over an inner join can still overflow on rows the join removes. That is the behaviour on main and is tracked separately.

## Example

```sql
CREATE TABLE products AS
    SELECT i AS product_id, 'category ' || (i % 20) AS category, 'brand ' || (i % 5000) AS brand, 'product ' || i AS name
    FROM range(100000) t(i);
CREATE TABLE sales AS
    SELECT (i * 7919) % 100000 AS product_id, i % 100 AS quantity FROM range(20000000) t(i);

SELECT category, brand, name, sum(quantity), avg(quantity), count(*)
FROM sales JOIN products USING (product_id)
GROUP BY ROLLUP (category, brand, name);
```

| | 1 thread | 8 threads |
|---|---|---|
| main | 2.01 s | 0.27 s |
| this PR | 0.31 s | 0.08 s |

(Release build, arm64, best of 5 warm runs, on a shared machine. The rows are identical.)

`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` at 8 threads, finest level of the cascade only (the coarser levels are the same in both plans).

main, 0.249 s:

```
HASH_GROUP_BY (rows=100000, time=0.65s) Groups: #0, #1, #2; Aggregates: sum(#3) EXPORT_STATE, count_star() EXPORT_STATE, count(#3) EXPORT_STATE
  PROJECTION (rows=20000000, time=0.00s) Projections: category, brand, name, quantity
    PROJECTION (rows=20000000, time=1.05s) Projections: #0, __internal_compress_string_uhugeint(#1), __internal_compress_string_uhugeint(#2), __internal_compress_string_uhugeint(#3)
      HASH_JOIN (rows=20000000, time=0.08s) Join Type: INNER; Conditions: product_id = product_id
        TABLE_SCAN (rows=20000000, time=0.04s) Table: sales
        TABLE_SCAN (rows=100000, time=0.00s) Table: products
```

this PR, 0.071 s:

```
HASH_GROUP_BY (rows=100000, time=0.01s) Groups: #0, #1, #2; Aggregates: combine_aggr(#3), combine_aggr(#4), combine_aggr(#5), combine_aggr(#6)
  PROJECTION (rows=100000, time=0.00s) Projections: category, brand, name, #3, #4, #5, #6
    PROJECTION (rows=100000, time=0.00s) Projections: __internal_compress_string_uhugeint(#0), __internal_compress_string_uhugeint(#1), __internal_compress_string_uhugeint(#2), #3, #4, #5, #6
      HASH_JOIN (rows=100000, time=0.01s) Join Type: INNER; Conditions: product_id = #0
        TABLE_SCAN (rows=100000, time=0.00s) Table: products
        PROJECTION (rows=100000, time=0.00s)
          HASH_GROUP_BY (rows=100000, time=0.34s) Groups: #0; Aggregates: sum(#1) EXPORT_STATE, count_star() EXPORT_STATE, count(#1) EXPORT_STATE
            TABLE_SCAN (rows=20000000, time=0.04s) Table: sales
```

The 20M-row join, the string compression of the group columns and the 20M-row aggregate on three string columns are replaced by one 20M-row aggregate on the integer join key. Everything above it handles 100k rows.

## Relation to #28573 and #28716

Both apply to the new case without changes, because it goes through the same code path:

- #28573: an exported aggregate whose argument can throw stays above an inner join. `sum(CAST(s AS INTEGER))` under a ROLLUP is not pushed, `sum(TRY_CAST(s AS INTEGER))` is (tested, with rows that only fail on the fact rows the join drops).
- #28716: the lower aggregate created for an exported aggregate gets the capped estimate (its input and the product of its group domains).

Float sums: as with the existing pushdown of a plain `GROUP BY`, the states are combined in a different order than without the pushdown, so a floating-point `sum` / `avg` can differ in the last digits. This is the same reassociation the pass already does, and that parallel aggregation does anyway.

## Tests

- `test/optimizer/partial_aggregate_pushdown_exported_state.test`
  - plans: the pre-aggregate is below the join for ROLLUP, CUBE, GROUPING SETS (with a fact column among the groups), with GROUPING() and HAVING on top, for LEFT / RIGHT joins that preserve the aggregate side, for an aggregate the query exports itself, and for every one-argument aggregate function the cascade exports;
  - plans that must not change: the pass disabled; no aggregate with an argument (`count(*)` only); arguments from both sides; FILTER; two arguments; DISTINCT; ordered aggregate; an argument that can throw below an inner join (and its `TRY_CAST` twin that is pushed); an aggregate that can throw below an inner join (and the LEFT JOIN twin that is pushed); the aggregate side not preserved (`dim LEFT JOIN fact`, FULL join); a non-equality join condition; an aggregate below the aggregate side; no group from the other side; a single group column; a many-to-many join, where a plain GROUP BY takes the double-eager rewrite and the ROLLUP gets exactly one pre-aggregate;
  - results with the pushdown and with the pass disabled, at 1 and 8 threads: NULL join keys, NULL arguments, NULL group values next to the NULLs of the ROLLUP, unmatched fact rows, a duplicated dimension key, an empty dimension side, a fact side that is empty only at run time (so the levels combine over an empty pre-aggregate), outer joins, INTEGER / HUGEINT / DECIMAL / DOUBLE / VARCHAR arguments, all supported aggregate functions.
- `test/optimizer/partial_aggregate_pushdown_exported_state_star_join.test`: a ROLLUP over a fact table joined to a filtered dimension and to the dimension that provides the groups (tpcds extension as data source, sf 0.01). The pre-aggregate sits between the two joins; rows equal to the plan without the pushdown at 1 and 8 threads.
- `test/optimizer/partial_aggregate_pushdown_exported_state_overflow.test`: a fact table with the HUGEINT and the DECIMAL(38) maximum on the rows of one key and a dimension without that key, `threads = 1` and `join_filter_pushdown` disabled. `sum` and `avg` under ROLLUP, CUBE and GROUPING SETS, and an aggregate the query exports itself, return the rows main returns (all sums 0) instead of an overflow error; the plans show no aggregate below the join, while the BIGINT sum and the LEFT JOIN variant are pushed.
- `test/optimizer/partial_aggregate_pushdown_exported_state_external.test_slow`: 10M fact rows over 2M keys under `memory_limit='300MB'`, so the pre-aggregate and the levels that combine its states run as external aggregates; same rows with and without the pushdown. A second part runs `min` over 800 byte strings (62500 states of about 50 MB per level) under `memory_limit='64MB'`: it only completes when the levels that combine states spill them, with and without the pushdown.
- `test/configs/verify_aggregate_state_export.json`: the first test is added to the list of tests whose EXPLAIN output differs under `debug_verify_aggregate_state_export`, next to the other partial aggregate pushdown plan tests. The skip "null pointer dereference when the partial aggregate pushdown optimizer encounters STATE_EXPORT aggregates" is removed: `test/sql/tpcds/tpcds_sf0.test` passes without it and `test/optimizer/partial_aggregate_pushdown.test` only differs in EXPLAIN text, so it moves to that list.

No expected plan or result of an existing test changes.

## Regression check

Same binary, the new case switched off and on (a local switch that is not part of this PR), release build, arm64:

- Plans: TPC-H SF1 / SF10 (22 queries each), TPC-DS SF1 / SF10 (99 each), JOB (113), ClickBench (43), at 1, 8 and 64 threads. Two TPC-DS plans change at each scale factor and thread count; no other plan changes.

title: Publish a runtime filter per key column for hash joins on several equality columns
body:
## What this applies to

Hash joins on a multi-column equality key where one key column on its own is selective, e.g. two fact tables joined on `(order_id, item_id)`, a line table joined to its parent on `(document_id, line_no)`, or any join on a composite business key whose build side has been filtered. These are common wherever tables have composite keys: the build side holds a small subset of the leading key column's values, spread over that column's whole range.

Today such a join only pushes the min/max range of each key column into the probe-side scan. The bloom / prefix-range filter of the hash table covers all equality keys at once and cannot be evaluated against a single scan column, so `CanUseBloomFilter` requires exactly one equality condition. When the build keys are spread over the range of the column, the min/max range prunes nothing, and every probe row is hashed and probed.

## What changes

A join on two or more equality columns now publishes one single-column bloom or prefix-range filter per pushed equality column. Each filter is sound on its own: a probe row whose value in one key column does not occur on the build side cannot match any composite key.

* The filters are built where the existing ones are: an in-memory join fills them while the hash table is finalized (per-column `PrefixRangeFilter` / `BloomFilter` next to the hash table's own, same lanes and build state), a join that is expected to spill fills per-column bloom filters during `Sink` from the join-key chunk, as the single-key path does.
* The choice between `IN` list, prefix-range and bloom filter, the build/probe ratio checks (`BUILD_TO_PROBE_RATIO_THRESHOLD`, `NON_FILTERING_*`), deferred publication and the selectivity sampling in the scan are the existing code paths, now per condition instead of for `conditions[0]`.
* NULL semantics follow each condition: `=` drops NULL probe values, `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` retains them.
* Single-key joins are untouched.

### Preconditions

A key column gets a filter when all of these hold; otherwise it keeps what it has today (the min/max range):

* the join type and key shape already qualify for join filter pushdown (no LEFT / FULL / ANTI probe side, the probe key is a column or a cast the scan can reconstruct, the scan is reachable);
* the build side is not larger than the probe side, as for single-key joins;
* the build side is not expected to hold more than half of the distinct values of the probe column. This is decided at plan time from the estimated current domain of the build key (the values the filters and joins below the build side leave, at most the build's estimated rows) against the distinct count of the probe column. Half is the pass rate at which the scan pauses a bloom / prefix-range filter anyway, so the check saves the build-side work for a filter the scan would not keep. Keys without a distinct count (expressions, aggregate outputs) are not gated; the scan's sampling handles them.

While working on this check I compared two ways of estimating the build keys. Capping the column's distinct count by the build's row count declines a filter that prunes when the build side is large relative to the key domain but holds few distinct keys, e.g. below a join that multiplies rows. The current domain does not grow with such a join, so that is what the check uses.

The rule has its own `OptimizerType`, `join_filter_composite_keys`, so `SET disabled_optimizers = 'join_filter_composite_keys'` restores the previous filters. Disabling `join_filter_pushdown` disables it as well.

## Example

```sql
CREATE TABLE sales AS
    SELECT range AS id, range // 4 AS order_id, range % 1000 AS item_id, (range % 97)::DECIMAL(10,2) AS amount
    FROM range(20000000);
-- 40,081 returned lines, spread over all orders and all items
CREATE TABLE returns AS SELECT order_id, item_id, amount AS refund FROM sales WHERE id % 499 = 0;

SELECT count(*), sum(s.amount)
FROM sales s JOIN returns r ON s.order_id = r.order_id AND s.item_id = r.item_id;
```

`EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, probe-side scan, before:

```
│ Table: memory.main.sales                                       │
│ Filters: order_id <= 4999980                                   │
│ Dynamic Filters:                                               │
│ optional: (order_id >= 0) AND optional: (order_id <= 4999980), │
│ optional: (item_id >= 0) AND optional: (item_id <= 999)        │
│ Row Groups Scanned: 163 / 163                                  │
│ 19,999,924 rows                                                │
```

after:


title: Convert the MARK joins of decorrelated EXISTS / NOT EXISTS into SEMI / ANTI joins once unused columns are removed
body:
A correlated `EXISTS` / `NOT EXISTS` whose correlation is more than a plain equality (a range or inequality between the outer row and the subquery, an expression over both sides, a predicate on the outer row inside the subquery) is decorrelated through a duplicate-eliminated CTE. Queries like "orders that have a refund larger than the order", "customers without an order above their credit limit" or "rows for which no later row exists" all have this shape. The plan that comes out is a MARK join between the outer rows and the decorrelated subquery, below a filter that keeps the rows whose mark is true (or false, for `NOT EXISTS`).

`FilterPushdown` already turns `FILTER[mark](MARK join)` into a SEMI join and `FILTER[NOT mark](MARK join)` with null-safe conditions into an ANTI join, but only for a mark that nothing references at the time it runs (`CheckMarkToSemi`). In the decorrelated shape the rewritten side still projects the mark up to an output that nothing reads, so the check fails and the join stays `MARK` + `FILTER` for the rest of the pipeline. The dead reference only disappears when unused columns are removed. A MARK join has to emit every outer row and cannot restrict its probe side: no statistics-derived range filter, no join filter pushdown.

This PR adds an optimizer, `mark_join_to_semi`, that performs the same conversion once the dead references are gone:

```
FILTER[mark](MARK[c](L, R))      ->  SEMI[c](L, R)
FILTER[NOT mark](MARK[c](L, R))  ->  ANTI[c](L, R)    if every condition in c is IS [NOT] DISTINCT FROM
```

It runs after `UNUSED_COLUMNS` / `COLUMN_LIFETIME` and statistics propagation and before `JOIN_FILTER_PUSHDOWN`. If a join was converted, statistics are propagated again (the same way it is done after the cost-based aggregate rewrite), so the SEMI join restricts its probe side. The converted SEMI join gets its null-safe conditions simplified with the existing `SimplifyNullSafeSemiJoinConditions` (now a static member of `FilterPushdown`). The mark expression is removed from the filter, and the filter goes away if nothing else is left in it.

### Preconditions

The join is converted only if all of these hold:

* the operator directly above the MARK join is a filter, and one of its expressions is the bare mark (SEMI) or `NOT mark` (ANTI);
* for `NOT mark`: every comparison of the join is `IS DISTINCT FROM` / `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM`, so the mark is never NULL (the rule `FilterPushdown` uses). `NOT IN` stays a MARK join;
* no other expression of the filter and no expression of any operator above it references the mark, and the projection map of the filter does not select the mark column;
* the join is a regular comparison join (not a delim join) without pushed-down join filters, and its right side does not read a `DELIM_GET`;
* the right side is not the constant list of an `IN (...)` (`CHUNK_GET`): the list is already pushed into the scan as a filter, and a SEMI join would only repeat it.

`SET disabled_optimizers = 'mark_join_to_semi'` switches it off.

### Example

```sql
CREATE TABLE orders AS SELECT i AS id, i % 1000 AS customer, i % 97 AS amount FROM range(20000000) t(i);
CREATE TABLE refunds AS SELECT 19000000 + i * 10 AS order_id, i % 89 AS amount FROM range(100000) t(i);

SELECT count(*), sum(amount) FROM orders o
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM refunds r WHERE r.order_id = o.id AND r.amount > o.amount);
```

Before (the part below the delimiter CTE):

```
FILTER Expressions: SUBQUERY
  COMPARISON_JOIN Join Type: MARK; Conditions: (amount IS NOT DISTINCT FROM amount), (id IS NOT DISTINCT FROM id)
    CTE_SCAN CTE Index: 18
    PROJECTION Expressions: amount, id
      COMPARISON_JOIN Join Type: INNER; Conditions: (id = order_id), (amount < amount)
        ...
```

After:

```
COMPARISON_JOIN Join Type: SEMI; Conditions: (amount = amount), (id = id)
  FILTER Expressions: (amount <= 88), (id BETWEEN 19000000 AND 19999990)
    CTE_SCAN CTE Index: 18
  PROJECTION Expressions: amount, id
    COMPARISON_JOIN Join Type: INNER; Conditions: (id = order_id), (amount < amount)
      ...
```

The SEMI join no longer probes the 19 million orders that cannot have a refund. User-mode instructions at one thread (`perf stat -e instructions:u`, median of 3, release build, rule disabled vs. enabled in the same binary):

| query | disabled | enabled | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| `EXISTS` (above) | 2.86e9 | 1.79e9 | 0.63 |
| the same with `NOT EXISTS` | 3.06e9 | 2.77e9 | 0.91 |

### Regression check

Rule disabled vs. enabled in the same binary on TPC-H and TPC-DS (SF1 and SF10), JOB and ClickBench: the results are identical at 1 and 32 threads (TPC-H / TPC-DS SF1); 5 of the 121 TPC-H / TPC-DS plans change at either scale, none in JOB or ClickBench. Instructions at one thread on the changed plans are between 0.94x and 1.01x; no query is slower than 1.05x.

### Estimated cardinality and the plan cost check

The estimate of a MARK join is the cardinality of its left side; the filter on the mark carries the estimate of the rows that pass. When the converted join takes the place of the filter it takes over the filter's estimated cardinality, so the SEMI / ANTI join is estimated like the `FILTER` + `MARK` pair it replaces. A filter that keeps other expressions keeps its own estimate.

The plan cost regression check (`scripts/plan_cost_runner.py`) sums the actual row counts of the hash joins of a plan and does not count MARK joins. A query whose MARK join becomes a SEMI / ANTI join therefore has that join counted for the first time and is reported with a higher cost, although fewer rows flow through the plan. In the example above (`EXPLAIN ANALYZE`):

| | rows into the join (probe side) | rows out of the join | rows after the filter on the mark |
|---|---|---|---|
| before: `FILTER` over `MARK` join | 20,000,000 | 20,000,000 | 45,353 |
| after: `SEMI` join | 917,519 | 45,353 | (no filter) |

The check counts 0 rows for the join before and 45,353 after. The join order and the build sides of the flagged plans are the same with the optimizer disabled and enabled; the only difference in the summed costs is the converted join itself. This PR does not change the runner.

### Tests

* `test/optimizer/mark_join_to_semi.test` (new): plan pins that the conversion fires (`EXISTS` -> SEMI with the filter gone and the conditions simplified, `NOT EXISTS` -> ANTI, a second conjunct next to the mark, two marks, both branches of a `UNION ALL`), that `disabled_optimizers` switches it off, and one negative pin per precondition (mark also returned by a projection, mark in the select list without a filter, `NOT IN`, mark inside `IS NULL` / a comparison / an `OR`, `IN` list); results for all of these including NULL keys on either side, duplicates, empty inputs, `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` correlations and VARCHAR keys. It also pins that the converted join carries the estimated cardinality of the filter it replaces, and that a filter with another expression keeps its own.
* `test/optimizer/deliminator.test`: two existing plan pins expected `Join Type: MARK` for a decorrelated `NOT EXISTS`, which is now an ANTI join. They accept `(MARK|ANTI)` now; what these pins are about, the SEMI join on the delimiter domain below it, is unchanged.
* `test/configs/verification_projection.json`: the new test is skipped in this configuration, because the synthetic projections it inserts sit between the filter and the MARK join.

The tests in `test/optimizer`, `test/sql/join`, `test/sql/subquery`, `test/sql/aggregate`, `test/sql/optimizer`, `test/sql/cte`, `test/sql/setops`, `test/sql/sql_export` and the TPC-H / TPC-DS SF1 answer tests pass, `test/optimizer` and `test/sql/subquery` also with `debug_verify_column_bindings` enabled.

This PR is independent of the other optimizer PRs I am opening next to it; they add entries to `OptimizerType` and to the pass list in `optimizer.cpp` as well, so they will conflict textually with each other.

title: Estimate a join on all groups of an aggregate as a key join
body:
A join whose equality conditions cover every group of an aggregate matches at most one row of that aggregate. The cardinality estimator does not use this. For a composite key it only has the FK/PK row-count cap, and that cap is skipped on purpose when a side has more than 8x the rows of the largest single-column domain (`CompositeJoinPairStats::CanApplyCap`, which keeps broad fact-to-fact joins from looking like key lookups). An aggregate over several group columns is usually on the wrong side of that guard, so the join is estimated through one column and the error multiplies with every further join.

The shape: two or more grouped subqueries joined on their groups. It is also what the rewrite of several `COUNT(DISTINCT ...)` over the same grouped input produces (one aggregate per DISTINCT argument, joined on the groups).

```sql
CREATE TABLE t AS SELECT i % 1000 AS x, (i // 1000) % 1000 AS y, i % 7 AS a, i % 11 AS b, i % 13 AS c FROM range(2000000) r(i);
CREATE TABLE f AS SELECT i % 1000 AS x, (i // 1000) % 1000 AS y, i AS v FROM range(100000000) r(i);

-- (1) 1M groups
EXPLAIN SELECT x, y, count(DISTINCT a), count(DISTINCT b), count(DISTINCT c) FROM t GROUP BY x, y;
-- (2)
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM (SELECT x, y, sum(a) s FROM t GROUP BY x, y) g1
               JOIN (SELECT x, y, max(b) m FROM t GROUP BY x, y) g2 ON g1.x = g2.x AND g1.y = g2.y;
-- (3) the result of (1) joined to a larger table on the groups; SET threads = 8; SET memory_limit = '8GB'
SELECT count(*), sum(da + db + dc), sum(v)
FROM f JOIN (SELECT x, y, count(DISTINCT a) da, count(DISTINCT b) db, count(DISTINCT c) dc FROM t GROUP BY x, y) d
     ON f.x = d.x AND f.y = d.y;
```

| | main (5ea088e855) | this PR | actual |
|---|---|---|---|
| (1) first join of the three aggregates | 446,370,930 | 1,045,083 | 1,000,000 |
| (1) second join | 382,869,037,248 | 1,045,083 | 1,000,000 |
| (2) join of the two aggregates | 482,297,215 | 1,097,624 | 1,000,000 |
| (3) join with `f` | 382,869,037,248 | 100,000,000 | 100,000,000 |
| (3) run time, peak RSS, spilled | 1.5 - 1.7 s, 8.4 GB, 353 MB | 0.6 - 0.8 s, 3.8 GB, nothing | |

In (3) main builds the hash table on the 100M rows of `f` because the aggregate side looks larger; with the estimate fixed it builds on the 1M-row aggregate. Same result.

### Fix

- `RelationManager::RegisterRelation` records the columns that identify a row of a join-order relation (`RelationStats::unique_key`): the groups of an aggregate with a single grouping set, seen through the filters and the projections above it as long as they pass the groups on unchanged.
- `CardinalityEstimator::ApplyJoinPairCap`: when the direct equalities of a join pair cover such a key, the row count of the key's relation is the number of key combinations, and it is used as the composite domain without consulting the 8x guard. If both sides have a covered key the larger one is used. The guard is unchanged for every other pair.

Not changed: joins on a single column, joins that cover only a part of the groups, conditions on an expression over a group, grouping sets, LEFT joins. A third relation joined to both sides of such a pair on the same keys is still halved by the unused-edge penalty, as it is for plain tables on main (three 1000-row tables with two unique columns joined pairwise: 500 estimated, 1000 actual).

### Tests

- `test/optimizer/joins/aggregate_key_join_ce.test` (new): the shapes above, a filter and a projection over the aggregate, and the cases that must not be treated as key joins (partial key, expression over a group, the existing fact-to-fact case from `fkpk_composite_key_ce.test`). Fails on main at the first estimate.
- `test/optimizer/*` including the slow tests: 327 test cases pass, no expected plan or estimate of an existing test changes.
- TPC-H and TPC-DS at SF1 (121 queries): every plan keeps its operators and join order, so results and run times are unaffected; one row estimate changes (a join on all three groups of an aggregate).

title: Use selective string reads before scan predicate evaluation
body:
When an earlier scan predicate leaves only a few rows, a pushed-down predicate on an uncompressed string column still reads every string in the vector before evaluating the predicate on the surviving rows. This wastes string materialization work, especially for overflow strings.

This PR reuses `StandardColumnData::Select` before `FilterSelection` to read only the surviving strings and their validity. A dictionary selection preserves the original row positions expected by the filtering pipeline. The change applies when both encodings support selection, neither column has updates, and at most 20% of the vector remains, reusing the existing selection-density cutoff.

### Reproduction and performance

```sql
SET threads=1;
SET force_compression='uncompressed';
CREATE TABLE t AS
SELECT (i%1000)::INTEGER k, repeat('abcdefgh',16)||i::VARCHAR s
FROM range(2000000) r(i);
CHECKPOINT;
-- Reopen the database, then run:
SET threads=1;
SET memory_limit='4GB';
SELECT sum(length(s)) FROM t WHERE k<1 AND contains(s,'123');
-- Result: 1619, before and after.
```

Change `k<1` to `k<10`, `k<100`, `k<200`, `k<500`, or `k<1000` for the other selectivities. Both predicates remain in the sequential scan.

| Rows surviving the first predicate | Before | After | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 0.1% | 26 ms | 7 ms | 3.71x |
| 1% | 26 ms | 8 ms | 3.25x |
| 10% | 29 ms | 13 ms | 2.23x |
| 20% | 32 ms | 22 ms | 1.45x |
| 50% | 40 ms | 40 ms | 1.00x |
| 100% | 48 ms | 48 ms | 1.00x |

Measured with identical Release builds based on `988d97f3153`, without extensions, using a single thread and warm cache. Results are medians of nine interleaved before/after rounds, with one warmup and three measured queries per process. CLI timing resolution is 1 ms. These measurements capture CPU and materialization savings rather than physical disk I/O.

Related: #24976 provides the selective overflow-string fetch infrastructure reused here. #28492 adds Select for fixed-size segments and does not address this string-filter fallback.

title: Run one-chunk task slices on the consumer of a parallel streaming result
body:
While benchmarking streaming result collection I noticed that `benchmark/micro/result_collection/arrow_stream.benchmark` (`SELECT * FROM tbl`, 25M strings, fetched through the Arrow stream result with 128K-row batches) stops scaling past about 8 threads: 0.56 s / 0.135 s / 0.10 s at 1 / 8 / 32 threads on main. The same query with a 64 MiB streaming buffer (`arrow_stream_64mb`) is faster at 32 threads on main (0.071 s), so the conversion itself parallelizes; the 10 MiB default buffer makes the difference.

#### What happens

Each unit a producer hands to the streaming buffer is ~8.6 MB (8 MiB data buffer, 1 MiB offsets, validity), so with the default `max_streaming_buffer_size` of 10 MiB only one unit fits and every other producer parks until the consumer pops. The consumer's loop per unit is: pop, wake a parked producer (its task is rescheduled and a worker is signalled), drop the array, fetch again. When nothing is poppable, `BufferedData::Participate` lends the consumer thread to production: `Executor::ExecuteTask` dequeues any queued task of the query - frequently the one the consumer has just rescheduled, before the woken worker gets to it - and runs it for a full `PROCESS_PARTIAL` slice of 50 chunks (~2.3 ms, most of a unit). Meanwhile every worker finishes its unit, one deposits it and the rest park on the full buffer. Nothing progresses until the consumer's slice ends and it returns to popping, so the pipeline stalls for a slice once per round of units, and from 8 threads on the row is flat: the workers idle most of the time while the consumer thread runs producer tasks.

The 50-chunk slice is the right granularity for a client thread that is the only executor (`threads=1`), or for a materialized result where producers never park. It is the wrong one for the consumer of a stream whose producers depend on its pop.

#### The change

The thread driving `Executor::ExecuteTask` while worker threads produce a streaming result whose producers can park (`ResultStoreCanPark()`, i.e. a streaming collector not settled on a retained result) now runs one chunk per slice and returns to its buffer. The bound is a thread-scoped RAII guard (`PipelineTask::PartialChunkBound`) set around the `Execute` call in `ExecuteTask` and read by `PipelineTask::ExecuteTask`, so:

- worker threads keep the 50-chunk slice, including the `PROCESS_PARTIAL` steps `ExecutorTask::Execute` runs while profiling,
- a client with no worker threads (`threads=1`) keeps the 50-chunk slice,
- materialized results and queries without a result collector are unchanged.

No new setting; the diff is four files, ~45 lines. The recursive CTE runtime's task has its own slice constant and is not touched.

#### Measurements

Interleaved A/B (main `ef9940daee0` vs this branch), `benchmark_runner --memory_limit=8GB`, medians in seconds over all runs of a cell (processes of the two sides alternated, 5 timed runs each), clang release build on a 192-vCPU arm64 box with other work running (1-minute load 20-40 for most cells, so the row-to-row absolute numbers carry some noise; `batched_stream_query` is bimodal on both sides).

title: Derive filter conjunct verification statistics from the input statistics
body:
With `debug_verify_stats` enabled, a filter with several conjuncts can nondeterministically fail verification with `Statistics mismatch: value is smaller than min` or `vector labeled as not having NULL values, but vector contains null values`. `StatisticsPropagator::PropagateStatistics(LogicalFilter &)` handles the conjuncts one at a time, and each conjunct narrows the column statistics (`UpdateFilterStatistics`) before the next one is propagated, so the verification statistics attached to a later conjunct assume the rows the earlier conjuncts reject are gone. `PhysicalFilter` ANDs the conjuncts into one expression whose `AdaptiveFilter` reorders them after warm-up, so a later conjunct is regularly evaluated over rows the earlier ones would have rejected, and whether the check fires depends on the order the adaptive filter happens to pick. 0f5722dc586 (#28275) fixed the same thing for join conditions; this does the same for filter conjuncts.

The fix propagates all conjuncts once from the input statistics, which attaches the verification statistics, and then runs the existing per-conjunct pass (simplification, pruning, narrowing) with attaching suspended through the `VerificationStatsGuard` the join code already uses; the guard moves from `propagate_join.cpp` to `statistics_propagator.hpp` so both can use it. The statistics derived for the filter output and for pruning later conjuncts are unchanged. `HandleFilter` gains an overload that takes the relation bindings captured before the first propagation, so `FilterBindingsChanged` still compares against the original expression.

Verification (reldebug): on main (5d254ad8707) the existing `test/sql/optimizer/join_condition_verification_stats.test` fails 4 of 5 runs under `--test-config test/configs/verify_statement_explain_sql.json`, whose SQL round trip plans the join conditions as a filter; with this change it passes 10 of 10 runs plain and 10 of 10 under that config. title: Write the leading zero for DECIMAL values without integer digits in to_json and JSON casts
body:
Fixes #28777 

### Problem

For a DECIMAL with width = scale and width > 15, `to_json` and `CAST(... AS JSON)` produce an invalid JSON number without a leading zero:

```sql
SELECT to_json('0.5'::DECIMAL(18,18));
-- before: .500000000000000000   (json_valid = false, cannot be read back)
-- after:  0.500000000000000000
```

Decimals wider than 15 digits are converted to VARCHAR and inserted as raw JSON numbers. The VARCHAR form of a DECIMAL(w,w) has no integer part (`.5`, `-.5`), which is not valid JSON.

### Fix

In the DECIMAL case of `CreateValues` in `json_create.cpp`, when width = scale, the new helper `CreateRawDecimalValues` inserts a `0` before the decimal point (`.5` -> `0.5`, `-.5` -> `-0.5`) before creating the raw value. All other decimals take the existing path unchanged.

`to_json` and the `ANY -> JSON` cast share this code, so both are fixed, including values inside lists, structs, and maps.

Not changed:
- The VARCHAR form of DECIMAL(w,w) stays `.5` (as checked in `test/sql/types/decimal/test_decimal.test`). The fix is local to JSON creation.
- Decimals with width <= 15 (written as DOUBLE) and decimals with integer digits.

### Tests

New `test/sql/json/scalar/test_json_decimal_no_integer_digits.test`:
- `to_json` and `::JSON` for widths 16, 18, 19 and 38 (every physical type)
- negative values, zero, the smallest and largest values, and NULL
- `json_valid` and reading the output back with `json_extract`
- nested lists, structs and maps, and column input

title: Make more bound expressions more immutable (Part 2)
body:
Followup PR to https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/pull/28704

# Motivation

See https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/pull/28704

# Changes

## `BoundColumnRefExpression` is now immutable

I've now removed `BindingMutable()` and `DepthMutable()`, so the only mutable accessors left are from the base class.

This required making some other minor changes in the binder/optimizer:

- `::VisitReplace` overrides in the aggregate rewriters return the replacement instead of modifying in place, or use `PreorderReplace<BoundColumnRefExpression>`
- `RemoveUnusedColumns` stores pointers to the owning expression slots/location instead of references to column-ref nodes, so it can replace nodes safely.
- `ColumnBindingReplacer` folds a chain of replacements into one new node at the end, instead of incrementally.
- Five places that changed a column ref's return type in place (type pushdown, scalar function pushdown, order-by binding) use the new `WithReturnType` helper to construct a new expression instead..

## Operator and conjunction expression constructors now take children

We had a lot of call sites  where we created these expression types empty and then immediately started pushing child expressions into them. We now pass children in the constructor instead, avoiding the use of mutating accessors.

- `BoundOperatorExpression` now has constructors taking one, two, or a vector of children.
- `BoundConjunctionExpression` now use the existing two-child constructor or the `::Create` helper.

We probably want to add more `::Create()` helpers in the future to make the different constructor calls more readable (or use some sort of factory).

## More Read-only call sites use the const accessors

Had the clanker do another pass on use of `.*Get()` vs `.Get*Mutable()` accessors:
- 62 `GetChildrenMutable()` calls that never mutated now call `GetChildren()` instead
- 34  other `Get*Mutable` accessors now also use their const counterparts

# Future Work

- `WithChildren` helper on all expressions, to re-create a new copy of an expression, sharing all the previous extra data, but with new child expressions.

- Port the optimizer off the mutable child accessors. This is going to be a more involved change so we may want to port these one-by-one. But the expression-rewriter probably has the most impact.

- The remaining followups from https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/pull/28704

- Probably use `cow_ptr` from https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/pull/28764 instead of `unique_ptr<Expression>`

title: Windows: trim core exports from self-contained extensions
body:
Windows builds reuse core object files for DuckDB's shared DLL and static archive. Their `/EXPORT:` directives retain otherwise unreachable core functions and dependencies in self-contained extensions. This change removes those directives from a separate core archive used by Windows extensions, allowing the linker to discard unused code and data from the final `.duckdb_extension` files.

The regular Windows CMake build creates `duckdb_static_no_exports` from the existing core objects without recompiling them. Its `POST_BUILD` command runs `scripts/strip_coff_exports.py` before dependent extensions link. The filter blanks `/EXPORT:` directives while preserving member offsets, the archive index, and other linker directives. Extension entry points and extension-owned exports remain available. Release extension links explicitly enable `/OPT:REF` and `/OPT:ICF`.

`WINDOWS_STATIC_LIBRARY_EXPORTS` defaults to OFF, so normal MSVC/clang-cl Windows source builds use the filtered archive automatically. ON restores the original core archive for extensions. The CLI and unit-test host keep the original archive; the shared DLL keeps the original objects. Prebuilt core archives retain their existing behavior.

Core extensions configure before the core targets exist, so archive selection happens during CMake generation. The final consumer also controls dependencies propagated through source and prebuilt extension archives. Dynamic loadables continue to resolve core APIs from the host.

Self-contained Windows C++ extension sources compile with `DUCKDB_API` empty. Previously, `/UDUCKDB_BUILD_LIBRARY` made these declarations `dllimport`, even though the core was linked statically. Without export roots, lld discarded functions/data referenced only through synthetic local-import pointers. Ordinary declarations give the linker direct references that retain the required definitions. `DUCKDB_EXTENSION_API` still exports the extension entry point, and dynamically linked extensions retain DLL imports.

The experimental comparison workflow and its size-reporting/batch-recording scripts have been removed. The PR keeps the CMake export-removal script and combines its archive and linking regression tests in `scripts/ci/test_linking.py`.

Earlier Windows measurements for the seven core extensions, from run 43388249656:

| Architecture | Raw MiB before → after | Reduction | Gzip MiB before → after | Reduction |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| AMD64 | 338.15 → 171.48 | 49.3% | 106.48 → 53.08 | 50.1% |
| ARM64 | 309.76 → 158.57 | 48.8% | 100.07 → 49.87 | 50.2% |

- Run 43410107284 on `ac838420ca3` passed both Windows jobs. AMD64 passed the unit suite with exports ON and OFF, then loaded all seven core extensions and the directly compiled demo in a host without statically linked extensions, ran queries, and exercised the DLL C API. title: Cost partial aggregation from complete grouping sets
body:
Double-eager partial aggregation currently derives a grouping estimate from the join output cardinality. With a low-NDV join key and an additional near-unique `GROUP BY` column, that can predict a useful reduction even though the lower aggregate retains every input row. It also assigns the same estimate to both lower aggregates and the reconstructed join.

Estimate each input’s complete grouping set and cost the reduced join separately. The shared grouping estimator excludes constant columns from damping, stays between the largest individual NDV and the input row count, and follows supported UNION/CTE mappings with bounded traversal. The cost check rejects selective joins before extracting input statistics where possible, while retaining useful asymmetric reductions. Aggregate states are bound only after the cost check accepts the rewrite.

This is the first part extracted from #28732. It is useful independently and establishes grouping estimates before the later join-selectivity and MARK simplification changes.

Measured `c75921481c13` against `331a01a177de`, using matching optimized builds, four threads, one warmup and five interleaved samples per query. Positive changes mean slower execution.

| Workload | Native tables | Parquet |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| TPC-H SF10 | +0.12% | -0.07% |
| TPC-DS SF10 | -0.09% | +0.71% |
| IMDb | -0.06% | -0.30% |

These individual differences remain unexplained; unchanged plans do not establish that they are noise, and this run does not establish which regression checks will fail in CI. title: Stage out-of-order in-place updates in PhysicalUpdate and apply them sorted
body:
## Problem

When an `UPDATE ... FROM` join emits the target's row ids in random order, the update is very slow:

```sql
CREATE TABLE tgt AS SELECT md5(i::VARCHAR) AS id, 0 AS v FROM range(20000000) t(i);
CREATE TABLE src AS SELECT md5(i::VARCHAR) AS id, 1 AS v FROM range(24000000) t(i) ORDER BY hash(i);
UPDATE tgt SET v = src.v FROM src WHERE tgt.id = src.id;
```

The hash table is built on `tgt` and probed with `src`, so `PhysicalUpdate` receives the row ids of `tgt` in `src` order. The storage handles each chunk one vector at a time: it splits the chunk into runs of consecutive ids that fall into the same 2048-row vector. With random ids almost every run is a single row, and each run:

- takes the table-wide statistics lock and merges the row group statistics
- takes the column update locks and merges one row into that vector's `UpdateInfo`
- pushes one `UPDATE_ROWS` undo entry through the transaction-wide undo buffer lock

On 96 threads this ran for 18.9s, of which 1040s of CPU time was spent in the kernel waiting on these locks.

## Change

- **Staged in-place updates:** `PhysicalUpdate` buffers the in-place updates of each thread whose row ids are not already sorted, up to 64 vectors of rows. When the buffer is full, and in `Combine`, it is stable-sorted by row id and applied in windows of `STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE` rows, so each storage call gets clustered row ids. For the query above, each vector then receives about 13 rows per call instead of 1.
- **Sorted bypass:** chunks whose row ids already arrive sorted, for example updates driven by a scan of the table, skip the buffer. Sequential updates are therefore unchanged.
- **Statistics lock:** `RowGroupCollection::Update` merges the statistics of the updated row groups under one lock per chunk instead of once per vector.

The DELETE + INSERT path (index or complex-type updates) is unchanged. `MERGE INTO` actions run `PhysicalUpdate` as a regular sink, so `Combine` flushes their staged updates.

## Results (96 threads, reldebug, shared machine)

| query | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `UPDATE tgt SET v = src.v FROM src WHERE tgt.id = src.id` | 18.9–26.7s | 1.7–3.7s |
| same, rewritten as an explicit rowid join with a kept `ORDER BY e.rowid` | 3.8–3.9s | 3.9s |
| `UPDATE tgt SET v = v + 1` (best of 7) | 0.038–0.087s | 0.045s |

The plain query is now as fast as, or faster than, the manually sorted rewrite. The sorted rewrite still uses less CPU (about 12s user against about 28s). It hands the storage fully sorted ids, but its single-threaded streaming `LIMIT` limits its wall time.

## Notes

- **Buffer is bounded by rows, not bytes:** the per-thread buffer holds 131,072 rows of the updated columns plus row ids. That is small for typical updates, but it is not tracked by the buffer manager, so very wide or string-heavy updates on many threads buffer correspondingly more.
- **Gain shrinks on larger tables:** the buffer size is fixed, so on much larger tables each vector receives fewer rows per flush and the improvement is smaller.
- **Error timing:** updates are applied up to one buffer later than before, so a constraint violation is reported when the buffer is flushed rather than at the chunk that caused it.

## Tests

- New `test/sql/update/update_unordered_row_ids.test` covers:
  - out-of-order updates spanning many vectors and row groups, for integers, strings, NULLs and structs
  - statistics after the update
  - rollback, and transaction-local rows
  - a write-write conflict
  - duplicate row ids
- Also run locally: `test/sql/update/*`, `test/sql/transactions/*`, `[storage]`, `test/sql/index/*`, `test/sql/upsert/*`, `test/sql/merge/*`, `test/sql/constraints/*`, `test/sql/returning/*`, `test/sql/delete/*`.

A SEMI join whose probe side has no columns returned no rows:

```sql
CREATE TABLE t1(c0 INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t1 VALUES (1), (2), (NULL);
```

title: Register casts in the stable API as a pair of scalar functions
body:
Removes the separate cast function API from the stable C/C++ API: a cast is now a pair of scalar functions of one parameter (CAST and TRY_CAST), registered as a cast.

```cpp
conn.RegisterCast(cast, try_cast, /*implicit_cast_cost=*/ -1);
```

## API

- Adds `duckdb_v2_{connection,extension}_register_cast(function, try_function, implicit_cast_cost)` (C++: `Connection/Extension::RegisterCast`). Each function needs exactly one standard parameter and a concrete return type, and no resolve types callback. Both must have the same types. `try_function` writes NULL for rows that do not convert and reports the error once the batch is written. The engine swallows that error and reports that not every row converted.
- Removes the `cast_function` handle and everything on it, plus `CastFunction` in C++. All of it was unstable.
- `CAST_MODE` moves from `function/cast.yaml` to `vector/vector.yaml`, since `vector_cast` still uses it. `cast.yaml` is gone, which is why the generated headers change.

## Engine

At bind time the cast binds both scalar functions with `FunctionBinder`, over a column reference of the source type, so their bind callbacks and bind data work for casts. The cast's local state runs each function's init callback once per thread. At execution the cast calls the function's exec callback directly, through helpers shared with the regular scalar function path. A try cast turns a reported error into a failed conversion instead of throwing. A cast's stability is the least stable of its two functions. Without a client context (when an index key is evaluated), the callbacks get a NULL context and the bind callback does not run.

- `CastFunctionSet::RegisterCastFunction` and `ExtensionLoader::RegisterCastFunction` take a per-cast `BindCastInfo`, visible as `input.info` while the bind function runs.

## Testing

The C API `[cast_function]` tests and the `Stable C++API: cast*` tests are rewritten for the new registration and pass.

title: Keep worker teardown and thread relaunch safe when an allocation fails
body:
Follow-up to #28656, which keeps the teardown of a query and the scheduling of its tasks safe when an allocation fails. Sweeping the malloc-failure shim of `tools/shell/tests/test_malloc_failure.py` over every allocation boundary of a `SELECT 42` run (the test itself only probes a handful of byte budgets, and the `test_malloc_failure_tail` case is racy on CI, e.g. run 43172067810, "Linux Release Tests") found one more place where the shell aborts instead of reporting out-of-memory.

## Problem

**A joinable `std::thread` is destroyed while the pool launches its threads (SIGABRT).** `TaskSchedulerPool::RelaunchThreads` started each worker thread before it had a home: the `TaskSchedulerThread` wrapper was allocated after `std::thread` was constructed, and the thread and its cancellation marker were appended to two vectors that could still reallocate. When any of those allocations failed, either the wrapper holding the running thread was destroyed (`terminate called without an active exception`), or `threads` already held the new thread while `markers` did not, and the destroy pass of `~TaskScheduler` then failed on `markers[i]` before it could join anything, so `~TaskSchedulerPool` destroyed the joinable threads with the same result. On this machine (192 hardware threads) that is a window of about 3600 consecutive allocation boundaries during `DuckDB::DuckDB`.

## Fix

`RelaunchThreads` reserves `threads` and `markers` for the requested thread count before the loop and creates the wrapper before the thread, so once a thread runs, handing it to the pool cannot fail. An allocation failure of the marker or the wrapper now stops launching further threads, exactly like a failing `std::thread` constructor already did, instead of leaving `RelaunchThreads` with an exception.

## Verification

All numbers are from the shim of `test_malloc_failure.py` on reldebug builds (Linux aarch64, 192 hardware threads), failing every malloc-family call from the N-th on, for every N in the given range; a run counts as a failure when it neither exits 0 nor 1 with an out-of-memory error.

| range of N | `main` (33e5799424b) | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 - 179999 (startup) | 1298 SIGABRT in `RelaunchThreads` / `~TaskSchedulerPool` (N = 45119 - 48722), 244 SIGABRT at N <= 244 (static initialization, before `main`), 1 glibc TLS abort | 0 in `RelaunchThreads` / `~TaskSchedulerPool`; the same 244 before `main` and the same 1 TLS abort |
| 180000 - 320300 (query and teardown) | 7 glibc TLS aborts (`GlobalUserSettings::GetSettings` on a worker, fixed by #28656), 2 SIGSEGV, 14 hangs | 5 TLS aborts, 2 SIGSEGV, 10 hangs (the same three kinds, which depend on the thread interleaving) |

* `python3 -m pytest tools/shell/tests/test_malloc_failure.py --shell-binary build/reldebug/duckdb`: 15 passed.
* `build/reldebug/test/unittest "test/sql/parallelism/*"` (79 test cases) and `"[api]"` (682 test cases): all pass.

A release build of the same `main` commit gives the same picture for the second row (142k runs: 38 hangs, 6 TLS aborts, 8 SIGSEGV, 1 heap corruption in `~DatabaseInstance`, no `terminate`).

Observed but out of scope here: a SIGSEGV / heap corruption in `DatabaseManager::ResetDatabases` during `~DatabaseInstance` after a query was abandoned with out-of-memory, and the `main` entries of the second row that #28656 addresses. An earlier sweep of a release build on an older base also saw `std::bad_alloc` escape from `~ExecutorTask` on a worker during teardown; that did not reproduce on this base in 140k-run sweeps of either build type, and nothing in that destructor allocates when profiling is off, so it is most likely the teardown use-after-free that #28656 fixes.

No new test: which allocation fails first depends on the interleaving of the worker threads, so the byte budget of the shim cannot select these holes deterministically; the existing `test_malloc_failure.py` passes on this branch and the sweep above is the coverage.

title: Read v1.x plans of struct_pack whose field lost its alias
body:
A plan that DuckDB versions before 2.0 serialized for a struct with a `count(*)` field in a correlated subquery, for example `SELECT x, (SELECT {'y': t.y, 'n': count(*), 'b': t.b} FROM o WHERE o.k = t.x) FROM t`, no longer deserializes: "Failed to find function struct_pack(VARCHAR,BIGINT,BOOLEAN)", which "takes no positional arguments".

Plans written before v2.0.0 carry the argument names of `struct_pack` only as the aliases of its arguments, and `RestoreNamesFromAliases` takes the names from the trailing aliases, stopping at the first argument without one. v1.x decorrelation (`RewriteCountAggregates`) replaces the reference to the count with `CASE WHEN x IS NULL THEN 0 ELSE x END` without keeping the reference's alias, so that argument has none and the arguments before it stay positional.

The fields of the recorded STRUCT return type are the argument names of a v1.x `struct_pack`, so for a function that takes only keyword arguments and returns a STRUCT with one field per argument, this takes the names from the return type. The new `struct_pack_count_subquery` case was serialized by v1.5.6.

This is a regression for plans written by v1.x, could it get the `backport v2.0-cyanoptera` label?

A plan serialized by v1.x with a `MERGE INTO ... WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET col = DEFAULT` on a table of a catalog other than DuckDB's own, such as Iceberg or DuckLake, fails on 2.0 with "INTERNAL Error: Attempting to initialize state of expression of unknown type!".

v1.x bound DEFAULT as a placeholder (BoundDefaultExpression), which the update operator replaced by the default of the column when it ran. Since #23033 the binder resolves defaults, but plans that still contain the placeholder are supported: PhysicalUpdate resolves it. Since #25228 the actions of other catalogs are planned through their regular INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE planning. The SET expressions of an update action are now evaluated in a projection before the catalog's update operator, so the placeholder ends up in the projection, where it can't be evaluated.

This PR replaces the placeholder with the bound default of its column before the projection. It mirrors the deprecated branch that #25228 kept for the insert action, which fills in the defaults of omitted columns of v1.x plans. 

Could this still be backported to v2.0?
