title: Read v1.x plans of approx_quantile over DECIMAL
body:
A plan that DuckDB versions before 2.0 serialized for `approx_quantile` over a DECIMAL column no longer deserializes: "Failed to find function approx_quantile(BIGINT)", or another integer type, depending on the DECIMAL's width.

In v1.x, `BindApproxQuantileDecimal` erased the quantile argument and then replaced the whole function with the one for the DECIMAL's physical type, which dropped `original_arguments`, so these plans record only the shortened argument list. v1.x read them through a fallback in `AggregateFunctionSet::GetFunctionByArguments` that took the first overload whose leading parameters had the recorded types; #25991 removed it. The existing `erased_arg_approx_quantile` case does not catch this, because its DECIMAL call does carry original arguments.

For an aggregate in a plan written before v2.0.0 without original arguments, when no overload matches, this selects the first overload whose leading parameter types and return type match the plan and completes the argument list with its remaining parameters. Matching the return type keeps a scalar call from picking a list overload. The new `erased_arg_approx_quantile_decimal` case was serialized by v1.5.6.

This is a regression for plans written by v1.x, could it get the `backport v2.0-cyanoptera` label?

title: `MarkJoinSimplifier`
body:
**Draft integration PR.** This is being split into independently useful changes, each requiring an overall benchmark geomean that improves or is equal within measured noise. The first split is #28766 (complete grouping estimates and partial aggregation); its latest head, `c759214`, is incorporated here. The next candidate is bounded runtime IN filtering, followed by independently validated uncertain-cardinality changes and the remaining MARK simplification. Later boundaries may shrink as overlapping work lands.

The performance tables below are historical measurements of older candidates. The refreshed integration branch has not been benchmarked again; #28766's independent measurements apply to that split only.

Related: #28786 targets overlapping MARK-to-SEMI/ANTI conversions after unused-column removal.

This adds a dedicated optimizer pass for MARK joins whose marker is filtered to a known truth value. Keeping these as MARK joins can hide opportunities for join reordering and runtime filter pushdown. `MarkJoinSimplifier` converts eligible cases to SEMI/ANTI joins while preserving projected markers, NULL semantics and evaluation boundaries. It runs both after filter pushdown and after IN rewriting/duplicate elimination, which can expose additional opportunities.

Exposing more filtering joins also exposed weaknesses in cardinality estimation. When the number of distinct values (NDV) is unavailable, using cardinality as the fallback domain can make an equality look extremely selective. Those reductions compound through join chains, producing unrealistically small intermediate estimates and poor join-order and aggregation decisions. This matters particularly for Parquet and derived columns without useful NDV statistics.

The estimator now floors each already-counted uncertain INNER equality contribution at 20% selectivity. Statistics-based NDVs and supported numeric min/max estimates can still produce lower selectivities. The fallback retains the original domain provenance and avoids counting redundant predicates again.

Grouping estimates also propagate through aggregates and materialized CTEs. Partial aggregate pushdown uses the complete grouping columns instead of reconstructing an NDV from a join estimate that may have been floored. It checks input retention and useful collapse on both sides; asymmetric collapse must save enough estimated join work to pay for aggregating both inputs. Runtime IN filtering preserves useful small build-side membership filters; numeric prefix-range and eligible Bloom filters take row-filter priority, while string prefix filters retain adaptive IN filtering for prefix collisions.

## Performance

The earlier local comparison measured candidate `09fa5fa` against baseline `c6f03c7`, before the subsequent cleanup and main updates. TPC-H and TPC-DS were tested at SF10, alongside IMDb, on base tables and Parquet, using one warmup and five interleaved samples per query with result validation. These are historical measurements, not a measurement of the current PR against current main. Geometric-mean runtime changes:

| Suite | Base tables | Parquet |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| TPC-H SF10 | -8.9% | -3.4% |
| TPC-DS SF10 | -8.5% | -8.4% |
| IMDb | -10.1% | -3.3% |

In that earlier comparison, TPC-DS Q54 improved **124→106 ms** on base tables and **242→177 ms** on Parquet.

[CI for `84948ad`](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/actions/runs/43186832924), compared with main at `988d97f` (including #27620), reports geometric-mean runtime changes of **+0.9% for TPC-H SF10, +0.8% for TPC-DS SF10, and +1.4% for IMDb**. These aggregates use the initial ten samples; individual changed queries receive additional confirmation. All three suites pass the aggregate CI threshold, but that does not establish a net speedup. Larger confirmed regressions include TPC-DS Q77 (**50.7→95.2 ms**, +87.9%) and IMDb 25b (**67.5→155.6 ms**, +130.6%).

## Known regressions and expected performance-CI flags

Performance CI may flag the following measured regressions, depending on its scale, configuration and thresholds:

| Query | Storage | Baseline ms | Candidate ms | Change |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| TPC-DS Q41 | Parquet | 39.9 | 61.5 | +54% |
| IMDb 03a | Base tables | 240.7 | 290.8 | +21% |
| IMDb 03c | Base tables | 318.6 | 359.0 | +13% |
| IMDb 05c | Base tables | 277.9 | 313.4 | +13% |
| IMDb 18c | Parquet | 1478.3 | 2123.8 | +44% |
| IMDb 29a | Parquet | 1009.9 | 1115.9 | +10% |
| IMDb 30a | Parquet | 1338.6 | 1706.0 | +27% |
| IMDb 30b | Parquet | 1077.7 | 1235.0 | +15% |

Q41 changes the hash-join build side. In 18c, the genre SEMI join moves later and the surrounding join order changes. Earlier profiling of native 03a/05c showed increased string-filtering and decoding work at the scan despite fewer rows reaching the joins. These explain the relevant plan/filter changes; exact attribution of every final runtime delta is still incomplete. In particular, 03c/29a/30a/30b have no isolated runtime cause. The 29a sample ranges overlap substantially; the other listed regressions have separated ranges.

The more conservative estimates avoid building the plan around extremely low cardinalities unsupported by statistics. They can also delay a genuinely selective join, and additional runtime filtering can cost more than it saves on some inputs. The earlier comparison showed gains in both storage modes, but the latest CI does not reproduce those aggregate gains, so the overall performance tradeoff against current main is still being investigated.

On [CI for `84948ad`](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/actions/runs/43186832924), the Advent of Code 2024 suite also regresses **14.7%** in geometric-mean runtime. Day 4 is the largest regression (**15.2→311.4 ms**). Its new join order combines grid cells on only one coordinate before applying the remaining constraints, producing about **30 million intermediate rows**. A focused comparison reproduces the slowdown with correct results: disabling join reordering restores the earlier speed, while disabling MARK simplification or partial aggregate pushdown does not. This is an additional join-order cost to weigh against the gains above; the individual cardinality-estimation change responsible has not been isolated.

CI's separate plan-cost check flags IMDb **03a, 03c, 05c, 06b, 18b, 18c, 21a, 21c, 25b and 27c**, and TPC-H **Q16, Q20 and Q22**. That check measures actual profiled intermediate/build/probe rows, rather than runtime or estimated cardinalities. Those flags describe the earlier CI revision; the refreshed draft has not established its current performance-CI outcome.

title: Preserve aggregate domains for proven singleton groups
body:
When DISTINCT ON is lowered to GROUP BY plus first(), aggregate outputs receive a cardinality-derived domain even when the grouping is known to contain exactly one row per key. This can distort join estimates although the aggregate preserves the input value.

Reuse child domain statistics only when the grouping covers a certified unique key and the bound aggregate has single-value identity. Reuse the existing functional-dependency machinery, preserve supported binding/cast lineage, and set singleton aggregate cardinality from the child. Carry identity through the ordered first/last/any_value rewrite, whose encoded sort key is non-NULL.

Nullable UNIQUE keys, deferred constraints, incomplete composite keys, lossy/TRY casts, multiplying joins, aggregate FILTER, list-returning overloads, and ordinary nullable-selector arg_min/max remain on the fallback. Tests include a concrete HLL false-positive case: 33 input rows are estimated as 33 groups although there are only 32 groups.

Related to #28615. This covers inputs with exact key evidence; it does not resolve the unconstrained CTAS reproduction. In the local 1M-node/5M-edge/5M-message experiment, repeated-query medians were about 29 ms for the declared-key variant and 149 ms for the unconstrained variant, with identical results. Serialized rewritten functions can conservatively lose identity metadata when rebound and consequently lose forwarding eligibility.

Validation on upstream main `39aeee12ef8`:

- `make reldebug`; formatting and `git diff --check`.
- RED before implementation, then 115 assertions in the new regression.
- 91 related native cases / 246,621 assertions with warnings-as-errors; the legacy arg-min case separately passed 62 assertions. Two TPC-H-dependent cases were skipped.
- New regression under three vector configurations and statement serialization: 115 assertions each.
- 32 notebook C++ estimate/result/serialization checks on the rebuilt implementation.
- Pre/post Z3 checks of the abstract domain-transfer condition; these establish the modeled invariant rather than verification of the C++ program.

The full test suite was not run.

title: Build Per-Column Runtime Filters For Multi-Key Hash Joins
body:
When a hash join matches on more than one key, the probe side sends almost every row up to the join, even when only a few of them can match. TPC-DS q93 is a good example. It joins `store_sales` to `store_returns` on both `ss_item_sk` and `ss_ticket_number`, and at SF10 its `store_sales` scan passes all 28.8 million rows to the join, even though only a small share of those tickets were ever returned.

Single-key joins already avoid this with bloom and prefix-range runtime filters, which the scan checks before rows reach the join. Joins on several keys only get min/max filters. The hash table hashes all of the key columns together, so a bloom filter over those hashes can't be checked against any single column. A min/max range on a key like `ss_ticket_number` covers nearly all of its values, so it rejects very little.

This PR builds a bloom or prefix-range filter for each key column on its own, choosing between them the way a single-key join does today. Each key column also keeps its min/max filter, and we skip a prefix-range filter whose build keys fill at least half of its range, since the scan would likely pause it anyway. The scan can then drop a row whose ticket never shows up on the build side. The bloom filters of one join split the size of a single bloom filter between them, so a join on several keys spends no more memory on bloom filters than a join on one.

Building these filters takes an extra pass over the build side, so we only build them when the build side has at most 5% as many rows as the estimated probe side; above that, most key values are on the build side anyway, and the filters would rarely reject a row. Single-key joins are unchanged.

Here is a two-key join where only `ticket` is selective. The build side is a 2% sample of the (item, ticket) pairs:

```sql
SET threads = 16;
CREATE TABLE fact AS
  SELECT (i % 300000)::INTEGER AS item, (i // 12)::BIGINT AS ticket, (i % 997)::INTEGER AS payload
  FROM range(24000000) t(i);
CREATE TABLE dim AS SELECT item, ticket FROM fact WHERE hash(ticket * 31 + item) % 50 = 0;
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT count(*), sum(f.payload) FROM fact f JOIN dim d ON f.item = d.item AND f.ticket = d.ticket;
```

Before this PR, the scan of `fact` only gets min/max filters and passes every row to the join (operators reduced from the JSON profile):

```
UNGROUPED_AGGREGATE          rows: 1
  PROJECTION                 rows: 480569
    HASH_JOIN                rows: 480569
      FILTER                 rows: 23999648
        TABLE_SCAN fact      rows: 23999680
          filter: (optional: (item >= 0) AND optional: (item <= 299995))
          filter: (optional: (ticket >= 0) AND optional: (ticket <= 1999996))
      TABLE_SCAN dim         rows: 480569
```

After this PR, `ticket` also gets a prefix-range filter, and the scan passes about a fifth of the rows. `item` keeps only its min/max filter, because most items are on the build side:

```
UNGROUPED_AGGREGATE          rows: 1
  PROJECTION                 rows: 480569
    HASH_JOIN                rows: 480569
      FILTER                 rows: 5167900
        TABLE_SCAN fact      rows: 5167900
          filter: (optional: (item >= 0) AND optional: (item <= 299995))
          filter: ((optional: (ticket >= 0) AND optional: (ticket <= 1999996)) AND optional: ticket IN PRF(ticket))
      TABLE_SCAN dim         rows: 480569
```

On TPC-DS SF10 Parquet, the `store_sales` scan of q93 now passes about 186,000 rows to the join instead of 28.8 million, and q50's passes about 125,000. I measured on a 64-core x86 Linux machine with 16 threads, against the same `main` commit:

| Query | Before | After | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| `multi_key_runtime_filter` (the example above) | 28.1 ms | 21.1 ms | -25% |
| `multi_key_runtime_filter_sparse` (a sparse key that gets a bloom filter) | 26.5 ms | 23.2 ms | -12% |
| `multi_key_runtime_filter_covered` (no key rejects anything) | 34.6 ms | 37.1 ms | +7% |
| `multi_key_runtime_filter_mid` (build side at 8% of the probe side) | 35.9 ms | 36.0 ms | 0% |
| `multi_key_runtime_filter_unselective` (build side at 17%) | 49.3 ms | 49.4 ms | 0% |
| TPC-DS q93 | 108 ms | 101 ms | -7% |
| TPC-DS q50 | 133 ms | 111 ms | -17% |
| TPC-DS q24 | 143 ms | 134 ms | -6% |
| TPC-H Q9 | 390 ms | 358 ms | -8% |

Across all of TPC-DS and TPC-H at SF10, the total time is about the same (-0.1% and -0.3%), and no query whose plan changed got more than 5% slower. I picked 5% by also trying 2% and 10%; at 2% the example above loses its gain, and at 10% the `_mid` build side gets the filters and runs about 30% slower.

The speedups are smaller than the row counts would suggest, since the scan still reads and decodes every row group and only drops the rows after that. A join that spills to disk still gets only min/max filters, because these filters are only built when every partition is finalized in memory. If there's interest, a follow-up could check the combined key in the scan as well, which would help when no single key column is selective on its own.

title: Share common subplans for multi-file table functions within a query (fixes #28218)
body:
## Fixes #28218: common-subplan sharing wrongly gated on statement-cache support for `LogicalGet`

### Problem

`PlanSignature::OperatorIsSupported` in `common_subplan_optimizer.cpp` rejects a `LogicalGet` for
within-query common-subplan sharing by calling `LogicalGet::SupportSerialization()`. For a
`LogicalGet` without serialization callbacks, that method returns
`function.bind && (!bind_data || bind_data->SupportStatementCache())`.

`MultiFileBindData::SupportStatementCache()` (used by `read_parquet`/`read_csv`/`read_json` through
the multi-file wrapper) unconditionally returns `false`. That flag exists so
`Binder::SetAlwaysRequireRebind` forces a prepared statement to always rebind - i.e. so a later
execution of the same prepared statement picks up newly-matching glob files. It has nothing to do
with whether two scans *inside the same already-bound plan* read the same, already-resolved input.

The result: two references to the identical `read_parquet(...)` call inside one query are never
recognized as the same scan, so the file is read (and, for aggregates, re-aggregated) twice. This
is a regression from 1.5.6, where the common subplan was correctly extracted.

### Fix

Stop applying the `SupportSerialization()` gate to `LOGICAL_GET` in `OperatorIsSupported`, and add a
narrower, single check in its place (`function.verify_serialization`, preserving the "opt out of
serialization entirely" escape hatch). The existing, more specific identity checks a few lines below
(declared-stability via `ClassifyLogicalOperatorRepeatability`, and "non-empty positional parameters
or serialization callbacks") are unchanged and already correctly scoped for this case - they were
introduced by #28324 for exactly this purpose, but were never reachable for multi-file readers
because of the gate this PR removes.

`LogicalGet::SupportSerialization()` itself is unchanged, so `Planner::VerifyPlan`'s unrelated debug
serialization round-trip check (`DebugVerifySerializerSetting`) keeps its existing behavior.
`Binder::SetAlwaysRequireRebind` / prepared-statement rebind-on-execute behavior is untouched.

### Scope note: read_csv

`read_csv` explicitly re-adds `.serialize`/`.deserialize` callbacks on top of the multi-file wrapper
(`CSVReaderSerialize`/`CSVReaderDeserialize` in `read_csv.cpp`), and both unconditionally
`throw NotImplementedException(...)`. That makes `HasSerializationCallbacks()` true for `read_csv`
(bypassing the parameter-identity check), but the actual serialization attempt inside
`PlanSignature::Create` then throws and is caught, so `read_csv` still does not share - a separate,
pre-existing limitation this PR does not change. `read_json`'s multi-file wrapper does not re-add
such callbacks, so it behaves like `read_parquet` and is fixed by this PR.

### Testing

- New C++ test (`common_subplan_nonserializable.cpp`): a minimal table function mirroring
  `MultiFileBindData` exactly (one positional parameter, no serialization callbacks,
  `SupportStatementCache() == false`) proves two identical calls share and execute once, and two
  calls with different parameters do not share and execute twice.
- `test_common_subplan_repeatability_readers.test`: flipped the pre-existing (and, per its own
  comment, deliberately-conservative) EXPLAIN assertions for `read_parquet`/`read_json` to expect
  sharing; kept `read_csv`'s assertion as "does not share" with an updated explanation; added
  negative controls (different files, different filters - must never share), a glob-sharing case,
  and a `PREPARE`/`EXECUTE` case confirming rebind-on-execute freshness is unaffected.
- `page_index_reference.test`: one pre-existing threshold (`sum(rows_skipped) > 10000`) had only a
  ~2% margin against the (buggy) baseline's redundant double-scanning and was legitimately pushed
  below it once this fix halved the redundant scans for that file's 5 test cases; recalibrated to
  `> 5000`, comfortably below every observed value on both old and new behavior, with an explanatory
  comment. Every other assertion in that file (page-index metadata correctness, filtered-read
  correctness) is untouched.
- Full `test/sql/optimizer/*`, `[optimizer]`, `test/sql/copy/parquet/*`, `test/sql/copy/csv/*`,
  `test/sql/json/*` and `[storage]` suites pass unchanged (~1588 test cases, ~329k assertions).

### Verification

title: CREATE EXTENSION REPOSITORY <host>: the host names its repository
body:
A repository created without a prefix is named after its publisher's host, and the host says where the repository is: https://<host>/.well-known/duckdb-extension-repo.json is the same metadata file a prefix serves, and only those fields are read:
```
{"version": 1, "repository_url": "<url>"}
```

From there on it is CREATE EXTENSION REPOSITORY <host> WITH PREFIX '<url>': the signing keys are fetched from the prefix and pinned. The fetch over https from the host is what makes the file the host's own statement; no registry is involved.

Repository names may therefore contain dots (not at the ends, not two in a row), and a host is spelled as dotted words wherever a repository is named:
Examples:
```sql
CREATE EXTENSION REPOSITORY carlopi.github.io;
INSTALL x FROM carlopi.github.io;
LOAD x FROM carlopi.github.io;
DROP EXTENSION REPOSITORY carlopi.github.io;
```
The built-in names stay reserved. A repository remembers the host it was resolved from, shown as the `host` column of duckdb_extension_repositories().

Repository `carlopi.github.io` is backed by https://carlopi.github.io/.well-known/duckdb-extension-repo.json, and repoints to the repository at https://carlopi.github.io/example-duckdb-extension-repository (whose duckdb-extension-repo.json file lives at https://carlopi.github.io/example-duckdb-extension-repository/.well-known/duckdb-extension-repo.json). That the repository and the extension are baked by the same host its due to convenience of github, but it's a coincidence.

Idea is that the ability to publish a `.well-known` file IS proof of control over an host.

allow_extension_repositories: 'undecided' (the default) lets a repository be created from its host; a repository by prefix still needs 'allowed'. The new 'known_hosts' value sits between 'allowed' and 'forbidden' in the one-way ratchet: only repositories resolved from their host can be added, and only those are trusted for install and load.

Reading a remote metadata file that needs httpfs reports a missing or non-autoloadable httpfs as such, for both forms, instead of a missing file. The debug setting debug_extension_repository_host_base lets tests serve hosts from a directory.

`INSTALL AND LOAD x FROM '<name>'` loads from the repository the install resolved, whether the name was given as an identifier or as a string; before, a string source fell back to a bare load, which never finds an extension installed from a user repository.

Known consequence: a v2.0.0 binary sharing the repository directory lists repositories with an error once a file with a dotted name exists, since it validates every file's name with the old rule; its INSTALL and LOAD, which look repositories up by name, are unaffected. Accepted.
